studies.title: Fulfil Your Bonds
studies.meaning: The surah opens with a single imperative and then immediately shows what it costs. Fulfil your bonds: the classical commentators read the word broadly, covering the covenant with God, the treaties a community signs, and the ordinary agreements of trade and marriage. What follows tests that breadth at once. Livestock is permitted, with exceptions to come; game is set aside while a person is in the state of pilgrimage. The closing clause locates the authority behind all of it, saying that God decides as He wills.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the later part of the Medinan period; surah five is generally placed among the last long surahs revealed. The community was governing itself, holding treaties with neighbouring tribes and administering access to the pilgrimage. The commentators report no particular occasion for this opening, and read its placement as a heading for the whole surah, which returns again and again to covenants kept and broken by the community addressed and by communities before it.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a knot tied tight. Arabic uses the same root for fastening a rope and for concluding an agreement, so the word carries the physical image of something bound rather than merely stated.
The verb means to pay in full, with nothing shaved off. It is the same root used for weights and measures given honestly, so keeping an agreement is framed as settling a debt exactly.

A state, not a place. The word marks a person who has entered the consecrated condition of pilgrimage, in which ordinary permissions are suspended for a time and the desert itself becomes off limits to the hunter.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian commerce ran on spoken agreement in front of witnesses. A caravan share, a grazing right, a marriage settlement, a truce between tribes: none of it was filed anywhere. The only enforcement was reputation, and a man known to break his word could not raise a partner or a loan. Herds were the currency of that world, so a rule about which animals may be eaten touched the household ledger directly.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah takes its name, The Table, from an episode that does not appear until its final pages, where the disciples of Jesus ask for a table set from heaven. Several long surahs are named this way, for a single scene rather than a theme, so a reader who opens at the first ayah meets contracts and covenants long before anything resembling the title.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing a command about contracts at the head of a surah makes agreement itself a religious category rather than a civil one. The obligation is not owed to the other party alone; it is owed upward, which is why the ayah ends with God's authority rather than with a penalty. That also explains the structure: permission and restriction are issued by the same voice, so what is allowed and what is withheld are equally acts of the same will.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same instruction and adds that every agreement will itself be brought forward and asked about.
Extends the bond to oaths sworn in God's name and warns against untying what was deliberately tied.
Continues directly, naming the sacred months and the pilgrimage offerings that the closing clause here has just touched.

studies.applyIt: Think of one small agreement you made this month and have quietly let slide, a reply you promised, a sum you said you would send, a time you said you would arrive. Do not renegotiate it in your head. Settle it today, and notice that the discomfort of finishing it is smaller than the discomfort of carrying it.

studies.title: Sacred Signs And Old Grudges
studies.meaning: A list of things not to violate, all of them markers rather than rules: the rites themselves, the sacred month, the offering animals, the garlands hung on them to show what they were, and the people travelling towards the House. Each is a sign that something stands under protection. The ayah then turns to the feeling that would make a person ignore such a sign. Old hatred is named and refused, and cooperation is defined by what it is for.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from one of the last surahs revealed. The reference to being barred from the Sacred Mosque points back to the year the Muslims were turned away at Hudaybiyya without performing the pilgrimage. Within a few years the same people who had turned them back would be travelling under their protection. The ayah speaks into that window, when the grievance was recent and the power had shifted.

keyTerms.note: From a root for perceiving and for a mark that makes something recognisable. The word covers both the rites and the physical signs by which they were known, which is why animals and months appear in one list.
Necklaces of bark or hide hung on an animal set aside for offering. They worked as public notice: anyone seeing the collar knew that the beast and the person driving it were not to be touched.
A word for lasting dislike rather than a flare of anger. It names a grudge that has had time to become part of a person, and it recurs in the ayah about testimony a few lines later.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The sacred months were the economy's breathing space. For four months a year weapons were put down across Arabia, and the great fairs ran under that truce, with poetry contests, debt settlements and marriage arrangements all timed to it. A collared animal walking a trade road was untouchable. Breaking any of these conventions did not merely offend; it made travel impossible for everyone.
studies.didYouKnow: The warning about letting hatred for a people carry you into wrongdoing appears twice in this surah, here and six ayat later, each time applied differently: once to aggression against those who barred the way, once to the giving of fair testimony. Repetition this close together is unusual, and the commentators read the second as generalising the first.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates a grievance from its expression without denying the grievance. The people who barred them are described as having done exactly that, so the wrong is acknowledged in the same sentence that refuses to license retaliation. Cooperation is then defined by content rather than by loyalty: the question asked of any alliance is what it is for, which cuts across the tribal assumption that you help your own.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same warning about hatred, applying it to the giving of testimony.
Describes the barring from the Sacred Mosque that this ayah refers back to.
Sets the limit of hostility, allowing kindness towards those who did not fight you.

studies.applyIt: Think of one person you deal with while carrying an old grievance, and check whether the grievance has started deciding small things: how quickly you reply, whether you pass on information they need. Fix one of those this week without announcing it. The concern here is not the feeling but what the feeling has quietly begun to authorise.

studies.title: The Day The Religion Was Completed
studies.meaning: A long list of what is set aside opens the ayah: animals found dead, blood, swine, anything dedicated to another name, and beasts killed by accident or by predators unless reached alive. Divination arrows follow. Then the register changes completely. A declaration is made that the religion has been brought to completion and the favour finished, and the hostile expectation of its collapse has ended. The last clause returns to the list and lifts it for anyone driven by real hunger.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the closing years of the mission of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). The classical commentators place the central declaration very late, most commonly on the plain of Arafat during his final pilgrimage, while noting that the reports about its precise setting are not uniform and preserving more than one account. The surrounding material addresses a community that now governed itself and needed its practice stated plainly rather than inferred.

keyTerms.note: The verb points to a whole that lacks nothing further, distinct from the verb used a clause later for a favour poured out to the brim. Completeness of form and fullness of measure are named separately.
A passive form: the person does not choose the situation, it forces itself on them. The word governs the whole concession, which is why the exception is read narrowly and tied to genuine compulsion.
Headless arrow shafts marked with instructions and drawn from a bag to settle a decision. Naming them alongside food places a way of seeking knowledge, not only a way of eating, inside the same list.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meat was scarce and rarely wasted. A carcass found on a trail, an animal that had fallen from a ledge, one gored in a fight over grazing: all of it was food to a hungry camp, and much of it was slaughtered at a stone altar with a name spoken over it. The arrows were drawn before a journey or a raid, at the same shrines. What the ayah lists is not exotic; it is the ordinary week.
studies.didYouKnow: The address to those who believe occurs sixteen times in surah five, more than in any other surah and more than in the whole of the second surah, which is more than twice its length. This ayah falls inside that run of direct address, which is part of why its central declaration reads as spoken to an assembled community rather than about one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Completion is claimed for the religion, not for the community, and the difference matters. Nothing further will be added to the guidance; everything after this is the work of understanding and living it. The clause about despair reframes opposition as spent rather than as ongoing threat. And placing a concession for hunger immediately after a declaration of perfection says that the completed thing bends for a starving person without being diminished.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same short list and the same concession for necessity, in the earlier Medinan surah.
States the list again in a Meccan setting, showing it was in place long before this declaration.
Repeats the exception for the one driven by hunger, with the same insistence on no intent to transgress.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of your own eating is done without a thought given to where the food came from or who it passed through. Once today, before a meal, pause long enough to name it: what this is, how it reached you, who grew or carried it. The pause takes ten seconds and changes very little except your attention.

studies.title: What The Trained Hawk Brings
studies.meaning: A question is asked and the answer widens rather than narrows. Instead of a list, the reply gives a category: the good and wholesome things are open to you. Then it handles the specific case behind the question, the catch brought back by a trained bird or hound, which the hunter did not kill with his own hand. The training itself is credited to God, who taught the human being the skill that the animal is now taught. The name is to be spoken over what is caught.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following directly on the list of what is set aside in the previous ayah. The commentators report that the question came from within the community: people who had lived by hunting with dogs and falcons wanted to know where the new list left them. The wording preserves the question rather than dissolving it, which is a pattern across this surah, where instruction often arrives as a response to something actually asked.

keyTerms.note: The root covers what is pleasant, clean and beneficial at once, so the word resists being reduced to a single test. It answers a question about categories with a quality rather than a catalogue.
From a root meaning to wound or to earn, used of animals that take game and of the limbs that acquire. The double sense makes the trained hunter an extension of the hand.
A participle built on the word for dog but applied to any creature schooled to hunt. It describes the handler, not the animal, so the passage credits the discipline rather than the instinct.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Hunting with a saluki or a hawk was not sport in that world; it was how a household ate in a lean season, and a well-trained dog was worth more than a camel to a family living at the desert's edge. Training took months of patient work and a bond that survived hunger. The bird returned to the wrist with the catch intact rather than eating it, and that restraint was the whole skill.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah closes by calling God Swift in reckoning, a name that appears at the end of passages about accounting and judgement far more often than at the end of a passage about food. Placing it here, after a concession, is the surah's habit: a warm allowance followed by a name that keeps the allowance from being taken for licence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two claims sit inside a practical answer. The first is that skill is derivative: what the handler teaches the animal, God taught the handler, so competence is traced upward rather than owned. The second is that a category can do the work of a list. By answering with the good things rather than an inventory, the reply leaves room for foods and situations nobody in that audience had yet met, which is how a finite text addresses an open future.

crossReferences.why: Describes the Messenger as making good things open and lifting burdens, the same movement from restriction to relief.
Uses the same word for the good things, addressed to all people rather than to believers alone.
Returns later in this surah to the same principle, warning against declaring off limits what has been left open.

studies.applyIt: Someone taught you the thing you are best at. Today, take two minutes to name them to yourself, and if they are reachable, send them a message that says what specifically you learned and where you have used it since. Not gratitude in general. One skill, one sentence about what it made possible.

studies.title: The Shared Table And The Dowry
studies.meaning: The permission of the previous ayah is restated and then extended in two directions that touch daily life. The food of those who received earlier scripture is open to this community, and theirs to them; the traffic runs both ways, which is the point. Marriage to chaste women of those communities is likewise placed within reach, on condition that the dowry is given and the relationship is a marriage rather than an arrangement kept quiet. A warning closes it: rejecting faith empties the work that came before.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a city where Muslims, Jews and Christians lived as neighbours, traded in the same markets and often shared kinship lines. The commentators do not attach a specific occasion to the ayah. They read it against the practical question it settles: whether ordinary social life across those lines was possible at all. The answer given is that eating together and marrying are not the boundary; belief is.

keyTerms.note: The plain word for what is eaten, without qualification. Its bareness is doing work here: the ayah does not carve out categories of dish or occasion, it names the whole ordinary business of feeding one another.
From a root meaning to fortify. The word carries the sense of a woman whose life is guarded and settled, and the same root supplies the word for a fortress, so honour and security share one image.
Literally their wages or recompense, the same word used elsewhere for reward. Naming the dowry with it makes the payment a right owed to her, not a price paid to her family.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina's households were interlaced. A date grove might be worked by one family and watered under an agreement with another of a different faith; a wedding drew in cousins on both sides of a religious line. Meals were the visible test, because a shared dish was the sign that two families acknowledged each other. Refusing food was how a community declared a boundary, so opening the table was a public statement rather than a private allowance.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for today opens this ayah and also opens the central clause of the ayah before it, two sentences apart. The classical commentators noticed the repetition and read the two as one moment, which is why the completion of the religion and the opening of the shared table are often discussed together despite belonging to quite different subjects.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah settles a boundary question by moving it. Difference of religion is not treated as contamination, so food and marriage cross the line, while faith itself is left as the thing that actually distinguishes. The closing warning keeps the openness from being read as indifference. The passage is generous about shared social life and unyielding about belief, and holding those two together is the position it takes.

crossReferences.why: Sets the same tone toward those who have not fought you: fairness and kindness are not withheld for difference.
Addresses marriage across religious lines from a different angle, in the earlier Medinan surah.
Uses the same word for the dowry, naming it as a right given to the woman herself.

studies.applyIt: Think of one household near you that keeps a different faith or none at all, and whom you have never fed. Invite them for something small this month, tea, or a plate of whatever you were cooking anyway. The point is not a conversation about religion. It is the ordinary act this ayah treats as unremarkable and most of us have quietly stopped doing.

studies.title: Water, Earth, And No Burden
studies.meaning: The washing before prayer is set out plainly: face, arms to the elbows, a wipe over the head, the feet. Then the exceptions arrive in order, the state after intimacy, illness, travel, the ordinary needs of the body, and finally the case where no water can be found, where clean earth stands in for it. The closing sentence explains the whole passage. What is intended is not difficulty but purification and a favour completed, so that thankfulness follows.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The commentators connect the concession about earth to an incident on a journey, when a search for a lost necklace delayed the company and left it without water at prayer time; reports about the details vary and more than one occasion is recorded. The general setting is a community frequently on the move, for whom the absence of water was a practical certainty rather than a hypothetical case.

keyTerms.note: The word covers the surface of the earth broadly, dust and soil and stone, rather than one substance. Choosing a wide word keeps the concession usable wherever a traveller happens to stop.
The same adjective used of permitted food earlier in the surah. Applying it to the ground ties purity of the body to a quality the passage has already been using for what is eaten.
A narrowness, the feeling of a space too tight to move in. The denial is physical in flavour: the passage says the intent is not to close a person in, but to open them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water was the axis of desert life. Wells were owned, guarded, and sometimes fought over; a caravan planned its stages by them and a miscalculation was fatal. Travellers carried skins that went sour and ran dry, and a party could easily pass a day and a night with none to spare for washing. The permission to use the ground was addressed to people who had already stood at an empty well.
studies.didYouKnow: The passage lists the washing and then spends its final third explaining the intention behind it, which is unusual: most instructional passages in the Quran close with a name of God rather than with a stated purpose. Here the purpose is given in the negative first, no burden intended, before the positive is named, and thankfulness is placed last.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Purification is presented as something done to the person rather than achieved by them; the verbs at the end have God as their subject. That reframes the washing as receiving rather than qualifying. The substitution of earth for water makes the point sharper still: if the material can change entirely without the act being lost, then what is sought is not the water but the turning, and the passage says so outright.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same concession in almost the same words, in the surah revealed shortly before this one.
States the same principle in another setting: ease is intended for you, and not hardship.
Says outright that no constriction has been laid on you in religion, using the same word.

studies.applyIt: Before your next prayer, slow the washing down by ten seconds. Feel the water on the back of your hands rather than getting through it. Most of us have made this the fastest part of the day, a thing done while thinking about something else. Notice, once, what it is like to arrive at prayer already paying attention.

studies.title: We Hear And We Obey
studies.meaning: Two things are placed together and asked to be held in mind at once: a favour received and a pledge given. The pledge is quoted rather than described, in the words the community itself used. Then the closing clause moves inward. God knows what the chests contain, which turns a public undertaking into something audited privately. The ayah does not repeat the pledge's terms at all. It repeats the moment of saying it, which is a different kind of reminder.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The commentators differ on which pledge is meant. Some read it as the undertaking given at the two meetings before the migration, when delegations from the city committed themselves; others read it more generally, as the commitment implied in accepting faith at all. The tradition records the range without settling it, and the wording is broad enough to hold both readings comfortably.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to bind fast, the same family as a tether and a thing relied on. It names an agreement with weight behind it, not an intention stated and then left alone.
An idiom for the innermost content of a person, phrased as a possession of the chest rather than a thought in a mind. It reaches what the speaker themselves may never have examined.
The verb has a reciprocal form, which places God and the community at the two ends of one tie. The pledge is not simply received from above; it is entered into from both sides.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An oath in Arabia was performed, not filed. Hands were clasped, a formula was spoken aloud before witnesses, and the memory of the gathering was the record. Breaking one carried a shame that followed a man's name into other towns. Poets kept the tally: a tribe's reputation was largely a list of pledges honoured or betrayed, recited at gatherings and remembered long after everyone involved had died.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase quoted here, we hear and we obey, appears elsewhere in the Quran as the answer of believers and, in an altered form, as the reported refusal of an earlier community who said they heard and disobeyed. The same two verbs carry both sentences, which makes the whole contrast turn on a single word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah pairs memory with accountability, and the pairing is the argument. A favour recalled and a pledge recalled are the same act of attention pointed in two directions. By ending with God's knowledge of the chest rather than with a consequence, it locates the pledge's integrity inside the person. What was said aloud in company is verified somewhere no company can reach.

crossReferences.why: Records the same words as the believers' response to what was sent down to them.
Gives the phrase again as the answer of those called to have a matter judged between them.
Describes those who kept what they pledged to God, and those among them still waiting.

studies.applyIt: Recall a commitment you made out loud, to a person or in prayer, that nobody else remembers. Do not judge how you have done with it. Just say it again to yourself in the same words you used, and notice which part of you flinches. That flinch is the ayah's subject, and it is more useful than a fresh resolution.

studies.title: Justice Is Nearer To Awe
studies.meaning: The instruction arrives with its own obstacle attached. Hatred of a people is named as the pressure that bends judgement, and the ayah does not ask for the hatred to be resolved first. It repeats the command bare, then gives a comparative rather than an absolute: acting justly is nearer to consciousness of God. The commentators note the modesty of that phrasing, which measures an act by its direction of travel instead of declaring it sufficient.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a late surah, in a passage that begins with the standing of agreements and moves through the treatment of those hostile to the community. Relations with several groups had broken down by this point, after years of raids and broken terms. The commentators record no single occasion, and read the warning as addressed to a community that now had the power to be unfair.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word whose root meaning is presence. A witness is one who was there, so testimony is described as reporting what you actually have rather than as advocacy for a side.

From the root for balancing two weights. The same consonants can also mean to turn aside, so the word holds equity and deviation together, which the ayah exploits by commanding one and warning of the other.

A comparative, not a superlative. Just conduct is placed nearer to awareness of God than the alternative rather than identified with it, which keeps the statement measured and leaves room for the difficulty.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Testimony in Arabia was a communal act. Witnesses were not strangers but the men of a clan, and their word carried the weight of the group behind it, which meant an honest witness could be accused of betraying his own people. Feuds ran for decades and everyone could recite the injuries. Being asked to testify accurately about a tribe that had killed your relatives was not an abstract test.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and 4:135 form a pair, and the pairing is exact. Each begins by calling believers to stand, each names a temptation, and the two temptations are opposites: one warns against being pulled by affection for yourself and your family, this one against being pushed by hatred of an enemy. Between them they cover both directions a witness can lean.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Justice is presented as something that survives enmity, which means it does not depend on the other party deserving it. The passage assumes a settled hostility and asks for accuracy anyway, decoupling fairness from goodwill. Calling it nearer to awareness of God rather than identical with it makes a further point: the act is no substitute for an inner state, but it is the closest thing available to a person who is not there yet.

crossReferences.why: States the same demand with its terms reversed, naming desire rather than hatred as the pressure.
Uses the identical warning about hatred a few ayat earlier, applied to retaliation.
Extends fairness to those who have not fought you, describing God as loving the equitable.

studies.applyIt: Pick a person or a group whose views reliably irritate you and find one thing they have got right. Say it plainly, without the softening clause that takes it back. You are not endorsing anything. The ayah assumes the dislike stays and asks only that it stop editing what you are willing to admit is true.

studies.title: A Promise And Its Opposite
studies.meaning: Two sentences, built as a matched pair, close the section. The first is a promise made by God, and the word for promise is used rather than a conditional: forgiveness and a great reward are stated as owed. The second describes those who refused and denied the signs, and promises nothing at all; it simply names where they belong. The asymmetry is deliberate. Reward is framed as a commitment God has taken on, while the other outcome is left as a description.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing a passage about even-handedness toward people one has reason to resent. Coming immediately after an instruction not to let hostility push a person into unfairness, the pair supplies the horizon that makes such restraint bearable. The commentators note no separate occasion for these two ayat; the placement does the work, turning an ethical demand into something with a stated outcome on both sides.

keyTerms.note: The verb of a binding undertaking, used in Arabic for what a person can be held to. Applied to God it makes the following clause an obligation He has placed on Himself, rather than a possibility.
The first word is a wage for labour done, not a gift. Pairing it with an adjective of magnitude keeps the sense of something earned while removing any proportion between the work and the payment.
A name built from a root for a fire kindled fiercely and heaped high. The Quran uses several names for the fire, and this one carries intensity rather than depth or duration.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wages in that economy were usually deferred. A herdsman worked a season and was paid at its end, a caravan hand on the return, a harvester at the threshing floor. Trust that payment would come was the whole basis of employment, and a master known to withhold could not hire again. Promises of future settlement were the ordinary currency of work, which is why a promise named as a promise carried weight.
studies.didYouKnow: The two ayat are close to the same length in Arabic and share a grammatical shape, which is why they are commonly recited together and treated as a single movement. The pattern of a matched promise and warning recurs through this surah, and it tends to arrive at the close of a section rather than at its opening.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing a promise and a description side by side says something about how the two outcomes are held. One is guaranteed by an undertaking; the other follows from what a person has done, and is stated without any language of obligation on God's part. The classical commentators draw attention to this asymmetry, reading it as mercy built into the grammar rather than added afterwards as a softening.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical promise formula and adds that God's word is the truest there is.
Sets the same two outcomes as a pair in a Meccan surah, keeping the same order.
Names forgiveness and gardens as the reward, using the same word for a wage earned.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you did this week that nobody noticed and that cost you something, a temper held, a favour done quietly, an honest answer that was inconvenient. Do not tell anyone about it. Sit with the fact that it was recorded anyway. Then do one more of the same kind today, deliberately unwitnessed.

studies.title: The Hands That Were Held Back
studies.meaning: A rescue is recalled without being described. A group intended to reach out their hands against the community, and the hands were restrained. Nothing is said about who they were, when it happened, or what stopped them, and the classical commentators offer several candidate episodes without settling on one. The vagueness leaves the ayah usable by anyone. What follows is not gratitude but reliance: the memory is given as a reason to place trust where it has already been justified.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Reports name more than one occasion: a planned attack while the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) sat with a delegation, an ambush prepared on an expedition, a raider who found him resting and was disarmed. The commentators record several and do not agree, which is why the ayah is usually read for its principle rather than its incident. The setting is a community under intermittent physical threat.

keyTerms.note: The verb of spreading something open, used of a hand offering as readily as of a hand seizing. The menace lies entirely in the object of the sentence; the gesture itself is neutral.
To restrain by withholding, as one keeps a hand from falling. The verb does not describe destroying the threat, only stopping it, which is a smaller and far more common kind of rescue.
A command in the third person, softer than a direct order. The form states what should follow rather than instructing an individual, which suits a conclusion drawn from something already witnessed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A raid in Arabia was decided quickly and executed at dawn. Camps posted watches, but the real defence was knowing which tribes had reason to come and which had given their word not to. Everyone had a story of a night that could have gone differently: a horse that shied, a scout who lost the trail, a plan abandoned for reasons nobody on the receiving end ever learned.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb translated here as intended describes a plan formed and nearly acted on, not a passing wish. Arabic marks the difference between settled resolve and idle thought, and the Quran uses this particular verb sparingly, most memorably of Joseph's moment of near-yielding, so its appearance signals an intention that had already hardened into a decision.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Protection is described as a restraint on someone else's hand rather than a shield around the protected. That locates God's action inside another person's choice, which is the harder claim. It also implies that most rescues are invisible: if the intervention happens at the level of an intention never carried out, the protected party has no way of counting how often it has occurred. The instruction to rely follows from that unknowability.

crossReferences.why: Records another moment when a threatened people answered with reliance and came away untouched.
Describes a plot to seize or expel the Prophet, and God's planning set against it.
Names another occasion when God turned back those who had come, without the community fighting.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing that could have gone badly for you this year and did not: an illness caught early, a journey you missed, a person who changed their mind about you. You will never know the full list. Take the one you can name and say something for it tonight, out loud, before you ask for anything else.

studies.title: Twelve Chiefs And A Loan
studies.meaning: A covenant is recalled in its original form, with its terms itemised. Twelve representatives were appointed, one for each tribal division, and the undertaking was given a condition and a consequence in the same sentence. Prayer, alms, belief in the messengers, support for them, and a loan made to God: five terms, and set against them a promise to cover over wrongs and to admit them to gardens. The final clause states plainly what happens if the covenant is abandoned after all that.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, opening a long section addressed to communities who had received earlier scripture. The Quran assumes the story is known and does not narrate it, which suits an audience in the city that included people who could supply the details. The recall serves the surah's argument about covenants: it has just told the believers to remember their own pledge, and now shows an earlier one and what became of it.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to bore through or to investigate. The word names someone who looks into a group's affairs on another's behalf, closer to an inspector than a ruler, and carries responsibility rather than rank.
A loan, not a gift, and the adjective means good in the sense of well made. The image places God in the borrower's position, which is startling enough that the commentators pause on it.
The verb means to cover, from the same root as a farmer covering seed with soil. Wrongs are not erased in the picture; they are buried, which is a different promise from never having done them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Lending in Arabia was a serious social act. A loan without interest to a man in difficulty was the mark of a generous house, and it was recorded in memory and repaid in loyalty rather than in coin alone. Tribes appointed spokesmen for negotiations who carried their group's word and were answerable for it. Both the twelve overseers and the loan would have read as familiar institutions, not as metaphors.
studies.didYouKnow: The image of lending to God appears six times in the Quran, always with the same two words, and always attached to a promise of multiplication or of forgiveness rather than of repayment in kind. It is one of very few places where a commercial verb is applied to God with God in the receiving position.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The covenant is conditional and says so, which distinguishes it from a guarantee of status. God's presence, I am with you, is stated before the conditions rather than after, so accompaniment is not the reward for keeping terms but the setting in which terms are kept. The closing clause then makes clear that a covenant can be entered and lost, which is this surah's steady theme applied to an earlier community.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same image of a loan made to God, and answers the question the image provokes.
Mentions the same division into twelve, in the account of the years in the wilderness.
Recalls the community's own pledge a few ayat earlier, which this covenant is set beside.

studies.applyIt: Lend something this week without keeping a record of it: time, money, a tool, an hour of listening. Then deliberately do not follow up. Most of us lend with a quiet ledger running in the background. Try one transaction where you close the ledger at the start, and notice how differently the giving feels.

studies.title: Pardon Them And Overlook
studies.meaning: A hard description ends in an unexpected instruction. A broken covenant produced hardened hearts, words moved out of their places, and a portion of the reminder simply let go. The passage then says that betrayal will keep surfacing, with a small exception noted, except a few of them, and instead of authorising a response it tells the Prophet to pardon and to turn away from the matter. The closing clause supplies the reason, and it concerns God's love rather than the other party's deserving.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, during a period of strained relations between the young community and some of the older communities of the city. The commentators do not attach the ayah to a single episode, reading it against the general situation instead. The exception clause is not decorative: it registers that the description does not cover everyone, and the classical commentaries are careful to preserve it whenever they summarise the passage.

keyTerms.note: Used of stone that has lost any give, and of a heart in the same way. The image is not of a heart turned evil but of one that no longer registers pressure, which is a subtler failure.
From a root for an edge or a margin. The verb suggests moving something to one side rather than destroying it, so what is described is displacement of meaning more than deletion of text.
Built on the word for a broad flat surface, which includes the page of a book and the flat of a sword. It asks for more than pardon: to present a smooth face and let the matter drop.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Grievances in Arabia were archived in poetry. A wrong done to a tribe was versified, memorised and recited at every gathering, so a feud could outlive everyone who started it by generations. A man who let an injury go risked his standing, since the reciprocity that protected a tribe depended on the certainty that nothing was ever simply dropped. An instruction to overlook cut against that whole machinery.
studies.didYouKnow: The two verbs at the end of this ayah, pardon and overlook, occur together several times in the Quran and always as a pair directed at the wronged party rather than the wrongdoer. The second shares a root with the word for a page, which is why the English idiom about turning a page happens to land close to the Arabic image.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction to pardon is not grounded in the other party's innocence, which the ayah has just spent four clauses denying. It is grounded in what God loves. That relocates the reason for mercy entirely, making it a statement about the one forgiving rather than a judgement about the one forgiven. The ayah also refuses collective condemnation in a single phrase, and places that refusal inside the indictment rather than after it.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction to pardon and overlook to the same community in the earlier surah.
Asks whether you would not love to be forgiven, and makes that the ground for forgiving.
Continues immediately with a parallel account of another community's neglected pledge.

studies.applyIt: Think of the grievance you retell most often, the one with a polished version you have told several people. Notice how much of the retelling is maintenance. This week, when the opening comes to tell it again, let it pass. You do not have to forgive anything yet. Just stop keeping the account current.

studies.title: The Forgotten Portion
studies.meaning: The frame of the previous ayah returns with a different community and a different outcome. A pledge was taken; a portion of what had been given as a reminder was let go; and the consequence named is not punishment arriving from outside but division within, enmity and hatred set among them and lasting. The classical commentators read the forgotten portion as the part that would have held them together. The last clause defers the accounting rather than delivering it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The community addressed here had a long history of internal division by the seventh century, and Arabian audiences knew of it through trade contacts to the north and through Christian communities in the peninsula's south and east. The Quran does not itemise the disputes. It names the mechanism instead, which lets the ayah work as a general warning rather than as a piece of reportage.

keyTerms.note: A share allotted, as of an inheritance or a division of spoils. Calling the neglected part a portion implies the reminder came apportioned, so letting one share go leaves a gap rather than a smaller whole.
From a root meaning to fasten glue to a thing, hence to make something stick. The verb pictures enmity adhering between people, difficult to separate once it has been applied.
An intensive form well beyond ordinary dislike, paired here with a separate word for open hostility. Naming both keeps the inward feeling and its outward expression distinct from one another.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian merchants travelling north to Syria and south to Yemen met Christian communities that differed sharply from one another and knew it. Monasteries dotted the trade roads, and travellers brought back arguments along with goods. A caravan hand could describe more than one kind of church without being able to explain the difference, and that ordinary awareness is the background against which the ayah's claim registered.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and the one before it are built on the same frame, a pledge taken and a portion neglected, with only the consequence changed. The Quran uses such close repetition sparingly, and here the effect is to make the difference between the two outcomes stand out against a sentence that is otherwise nearly identical.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Division is presented as a consequence rather than an accident, and the mechanism given is neglect rather than rebellion. Nothing is described as being denied outright; something was simply allowed to slip. That makes the warning harder to escape, since neglect requires no decision at any point. Deferring the verdict to the last day, rather than issuing it here, also keeps the passage from being used as a judgement on any living person.

crossReferences.why: Names holding together to the rope of God as precisely what prevents the outcome described here.
Says division came after knowledge arrived, out of rivalry between them rather than ignorance.
Sets up the frame this ayah repeats, using the same words for the neglected portion.

studies.applyIt: Pick something you learned once and know you have let go: a language, a practice, a discipline you were good at. Do not try to restore it. Just spend fifteen minutes with it this week and notice how much is still there. This ayah is about portions dropped quietly, and most of ours are dropped without a decision.

studies.title: A Light And A Clear Book
studies.meaning: An address is made directly to those who hold earlier scripture, and it is framed as arrival rather than accusation. The messenger clarifies much of what had been kept concealed and, this is the striking half, passes over much else. Deliberate silence is named as part of the mission. Then the sentence turns to what has come: a light, and a book that makes things plain. The two are given without an explicit link, and the commentators differ on whether the light names the messenger or the revelation.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the section of the surah addressed to communities holding earlier scripture. The commentators report no specific occasion. The setting is a city where scriptural learning was present and where questions about what a text said, and what had been left out of public teaching, were live and often argued. The ayah enters that conversation as a claim about disclosure rather than as a demand.

keyTerms.note: Indefinite in the Arabic, so a light rather than the light. The commentators read it as the messenger or as the revelation, and the indefiniteness is part of why the question stays open.
An active participle, so the book is not merely clear but clarifying: it does something to what it touches. The same root supplies the verb used two clauses earlier for the messenger's work.

The verb of pardoning, used here of information rather than of offence. It describes leaving something undisclosed as an act of forbearance, which is unusual to praise in a passage about clarification.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Scripture in seventh-century Arabia was largely heard, not read. Texts lived with the scholars who held them, were recited in gatherings, and reached ordinary people through teachers who chose what to pass on. Literacy was rare and manuscripts rarer, so what a community knew of its own book depended heavily on a small number of people. A claim about what had been kept back was, in that setting, a claim about those people.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and one four later open with the same address and the same phrase about a messenger who has come, forming a bracket around the material between them. The surah uses that kind of repeated opening several times, which gives its long middle section a shape audible in recitation before it becomes visible on a page.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is described here as disclosure with restraint, and the restraint is credited rather than apologised for. That says something about how the Quran understands its own scope: it does not claim to settle every question a reader might bring, and it treats some silences as mercy. The ayah also frames the encounter between communities as one about information rather than power, which sets the terms for the passage that follows.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the address and the arrival, moving the emphasis to the long gap that preceded it.
Calls the revelation a light by which God guides whom He wills, using the same image.
Speaks of a covenant to make the scripture clear to people and not to conceal it.

studies.applyIt: There is something you know about someone that you could say and have not said. Check, once, which kind of silence it is: protection, or avoidance. This ayah praises one and not the other, and the difference is usually obvious to you and to nobody else. You do not need to act today. Just name it accurately.

studies.title: The Ways Of Peace
studies.meaning: The light of the previous sentence is given a function here, and it is described as movement rather than illumination. God guides by it those who follow what pleases Him along the roads of peace, and brings them out of darkness into light. The plural is worth noticing: darknesses, several, against a single light. The passage ends with a straight path, so three images of direction are stacked in one sentence without any of them being explained.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the address to communities holding earlier scripture. No specific occasion is reported. The passage arrives at a point in the surah where the argument has been about disclosure and concealment, and it answers the question left hanging: what the newly arrived light is for. The community in the city was itself newly assembled out of tribes that had fought each other, so roads of peace was not an abstraction.

keyTerms.note: A plural of paths, not one road. The second word covers peace, soundness and safety together, and is also a name of God, so the phrase can be heard as the roads that lead to Him.
Plural in Arabic where English has only a singular. Darkness comes in kinds and layers; light in this sentence stays single, and the imbalance is a regular feature of the Quran's use of the pair.

An intensive form of contentment, used almost exclusively of God's acceptance. What is followed here is not a rule but an inclination, which makes the condition attached to guidance one of orientation rather than performance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A route across Arabia was chosen for safety before speed. Some wadis were held by tribes with a grudge, some wells had a price, and a guide's whole value was knowing which was which this season. Caravans travelled by night under stars they had learned by name, and a wrong turn in the dark meant days lost or worse. Peace and road were practically the same word to a traveller.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran pairs darkness with light thirteen times, and in every one of them darkness is plural in the Arabic while light stays singular. The plural form of the word for light never occurs in the text at all. English translations smooth this out because a plural darkness reads awkwardly, so a reader working from a translation rarely meets the pattern.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Guidance is described as something done to a person who has already turned, which places human inclination before divine direction without making it the cause. The clause by His permission sits in the middle and keeps the movement from being automatic. And peace is named as the destination of the roads rather than as their condition, which reverses the usual assumption that a person must be at peace before setting out.

crossReferences.why: Describes God as the ally who brings believers out of darkness into light, in the same words.
Opens by naming the book's purpose as bringing people out of darkness into light.
Says God and His angels do this for the believers, adding mercy as the motive.

studies.applyIt: Think of a disagreement you are in that has more than one way forward. List the routes honestly, including the one that costs you something. Then ask which of them ends with everyone still speaking. That is the only test this ayah offers, and it usually rules out the option you had already decided on.

studies.title: Who Could Prevent God
studies.meaning: A specific claim is named and rejected: that God is the Messiah, son of Mary. The refutation is not an argument from scripture but from a single question. If God willed to bring the Messiah to an end, along with his mother and everyone on earth, who could hold Him back? Naming the mother beside the son places both inside the created order. The sentence then widens to sovereignty over the heavens and the earth, and to a creating that answers to nothing outside itself.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the surah's long address to communities holding earlier scripture. Christian communities were present in Arabia, at Najran in the south and along the northern trade routes, and delegations reached the city. The commentators do not tie the ayah to one meeting. It engages a particular formulation rather than a whole community, which is why the phrasing is precise about exactly what is being denied.

keyTerms.note: The Quran keeps this title throughout and never disputes it; what it disputes is what the title is taken to mean. The word appears twice in this one sentence, both times with the son of Mary attached.
The verb of ownership rather than of strength. The question asks who possesses anything at all against God, which turns a debate about nature into a question about property and control.

keyTerms.gloss: to destroy, bring to an end
keyTerms.note: A verb used of perishing and of being lost. Applying it hypothetically tests the claim by asking what would follow if the one being called God could cease, which is the whole argument compressed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia knew Christianity through monks on the caravan roads, through the church at Najran with its own bishops, and through Abyssinia across the sea, where a Christian king had sheltered emigrants from Mecca. Traders carried theological disputes north and south along with incense and cloth. The formulations argued over in Syrian and Ethiopian churches were not distant abstractions; they arrived in the market with the goods.
studies.didYouKnow: Mary is the only woman named in the Quran, and Jesus is nearly always identified as her son rather than through a father's line, including in passages that dispute claims made about him. The nineteenth surah carries her name and gives her story at greater length than any other passage in the text.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument turns on contingency rather than on scripture, which makes it available to anyone. Whatever can be brought to an end is not the one who ends things; whatever entered existence through birth has a beginning. By adding everyone on earth to the same clause, the ayah refuses to single anyone out: the Messiah's createdness is stated as the shared condition of all created things rather than as a demotion of him in particular.

crossReferences.why: Returns to the same claim later in this surah and adds the Messiah's own words about worship.
Compares the creation of Jesus to that of Adam, made from dust by a word.
Gives Jesus describing himself as a servant of God, in his own reported speech.

studies.applyIt: If you have a Christian friend or colleague, ask them sometime what they actually believe, in their own words, rather than what you have heard about it. Listen without correcting. This ayah is precise about the formulation it addresses, and precision is impossible if you have only ever heard a position described by people who reject it.

studies.title: Then Why Does He Punish You
studies.meaning: A claim of special standing is quoted and answered with a question rather than a denial. If you are the children of God and His beloved, why then are you punished for your wrongs? The answer given is short and deflationary: you are human beings from among those He created. What follows removes the last footing for the claim by placing forgiveness and punishment entirely within God's will, and then widens to sovereignty and return, so nothing is left resting on inherited status.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, within the surah's address to communities of earlier scripture. The classical commentators report that a version of the claim was made in conversation with the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) in the city, though the reports differ in their details. The wider setting is a society where communal identity was inherited and rarely questioned, and where a claim of favour by descent sounded ordinary rather than provocative.

keyTerms.note: A plural of the intensive form, so considerably more than fondness. Pairing it with the claim of sonship shows what was at stake: not affection but a standing that no conduct could put at risk.
The word for the human as flesh and skin, distinct from the term that emphasises companionship or forgetting. It is the plainest available way of saying you are made of what everyone else is made of.
A noun of place from a verb meaning to become. It names not simply where one arrives but what one turns into on arriving, which is why it closes passages about accountability.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Descent was the load-bearing structure of Arabian society. A man's genealogy was recited before his name in formal settings, and it determined whom he could marry, what protection he could claim, and where he sat at a gathering. Claims of inherited favour were the ordinary grammar of status. The reply here, that you are human beings from among those He created, dismantles a whole social architecture in a single short clause.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah answers a claim with a question and never states the counter-position directly; the correction arrives entirely through what the listener has to concede. This is a recurring method in the surah, which prefers to argue by asking rather than by declaring, and it is part of why several of its passages read as one side of a live conversation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates being loved from being exempt. It does not deny that God loves; this surah says elsewhere that He will bring a people He loves and who love Him. What it denies is that love can be inherited, or that it suspends consequence. Placing forgiveness and punishment together under a single will keeps both hope and accountability alive without letting either harden into a possession.

crossReferences.why: Answers another claim of exclusive entry with a demand for proof rather than a flat denial.
Speaks of a people God loves and who love Him, showing love described but never inherited.
States that outcomes follow deeds rather than the wishes of any community about itself.

studies.applyIt: Find the place where you assume you get some latitude, because of your family, your record, how long you have been doing this, how much you have given. Say the assumption out loud to yourself in one sentence. You do not need to dismantle it today. Most of us have never even heard ours stated plainly.

studies.title: After A Long Silence
studies.meaning: The address of a few ayat earlier returns, this time with a different emphasis. A messenger has come, and the phrase that matters is the one about a gap: after an interval in which no messenger came. The purpose is stated as pre-emption, so that you cannot say nobody came to us. Then the two functions are named, bringer of good news and warner, and immediately repeated in the affirmative. Nothing is argued here. A gap is closed and the record set straight.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The interval referred to is the stretch between Jesus and the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), reckoned in the classical sources at several centuries, though the figures the commentators give differ from one another. Arabia across that period held prophetic memory but no prophetic presence of its own, which is part of why the region features so little in the scriptural histories the surrounding communities preserved.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to slacken or fall quiet after activity. It names a pause in something ongoing rather than a simple absence, which frames the gap as an interruption within a sequence.
From the root for skin, because news that pleases shows first in the face. The word names the effect on the hearer rather than the content of what is carried.
One who gives notice of something coming while there is still time to act on it. The Arabic carries urgency without threat; a warner in this sense performs a service rather than a punishment.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: News in Arabia arrived on foot. A rider reaching an encampment was surrounded before he dismounted, and what he carried, a raid, a death, a market price, a birth, was repeated and turned over for days afterwards. The one who came with good news was rewarded with a gift by custom. Both of the words in this ayah name roles that existed in that society and were paid for.
studies.didYouKnow: The two titles paired here, bringer of good news and warner, recur throughout the Quran whenever a messenger's role is being defined, and are only rarely used alone. In this ayah they appear twice inside a single sentence: once within the objection being pre-empted, and then again in the affirmation that answers it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah treats the absence of guidance as an argument a person could genuinely make, and takes it seriously enough to close. That implies accountability is tied to access: nobody is held to what never reached them. It also frames revelation as a response to a possible complaint rather than as an imposition, which changes the posture of the whole encounter from demand to answer.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle: messengers sent so people have no argument against God afterwards.
Says no community is called to account until a messenger has been sent to it.
Opens with the same address and the same arrival, with its emphasis on disclosure instead.

studies.applyIt: Think of an excuse you keep in reserve: nobody told me, I was never taught, it was not explained. Test one of them honestly this week by finding out whether the information was actually available to you. Sometimes it was not, and that matters. Often it was, and knowing which is which is worth the half hour.

studies.title: Prophets, Kings, And A Land
studies.meaning: Moses opens by counting the favours before making the demand, and the order matters. Prophets among you, kingship, and a gift given to no other people: three items, none of them the land. Then the instruction arrives, framed as entry into something already assigned rather than conquest of something new. The warning attached is not about failure but about turning back, which is a different risk entirely, and the loss named is what that turning would cost them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, and the Quran is retelling a history its audience partly knew. The episode belongs to the years after the escape from Egypt, at the threshold of the land. The passage sits in this surah directly after the covenant recalled at its opening, so a broken pledge and a refused instruction stand a few ayat apart. The commentators treat that sequence as the surah's argument rather than as chronology.

keyTerms.note: The commentators read the plural several ways: rulers in fact, or people freed from serving anyone, or households with a home and a servant of their own. Every reading turns on ownership of one's own life.
A passive participle from a root meaning to be pure and to be set aside. The land is not called holy in itself but made so, which keeps the sanctity a matter of designation.
The verb of a reversal, physically retreating the way one came. It is the same word used elsewhere for abandoning faith, so the image of walking backwards carries both senses at once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: For an Arabian audience, entering land held by others was an entirely familiar prospect and an entirely frightening one. Settled towns had walls, wells and stored grain; nomadic groups had mobility and little to defend. A decision to move on a fortified place was taken by consultation and could split a tribe, because the ones who went were rarely the ones who had argued for it. Reluctance here needed no explanation.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the few places where the Quran gives a speech of Moses to his own people with no confrontation with Pharaoh anywhere near it. Most of the Moses material is built around the contest in Egypt; this passage belongs to the harder, later story, and the surah reaches for it because its subject is covenant rather than deliverance.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The favour is recited before the demand, which sets a pattern: what is asked of a community is presented as proportionate to what it has already received. Naming the land as written for them makes the instruction a matter of taking possession rather than of gambling, and that is exactly what the refusal in the next ayah will not accept. Assurance, the passage implies, does not remove the need to walk.

crossReferences.why: Gives the reply immediately, and the refusal turns on exactly the assurance offered here.
Describes the inheritance of the land promised, within a passage on the same history.
Recalls the same favour, being preferred over the worlds, at the start of the longest surah.

studies.applyIt: Before you next ask someone for something difficult, spend a minute listing what they have already given you, and say one item of it aloud when you ask. Not as technique. The order in this passage is favour first, demand second, and most requests fail because they arrive with the second half only.

studies.title: Not Until They Leave
studies.meaning: The refusal is careful, and that is what makes it damning. They do not deny the promise or the prophet; they attach a condition. There are overpowering people in it, so we will not enter until they leave, and if they leave we will enter. The logic is impeccable and empty: they will take the land at precisely the moment it needs no taking. Faith is not rejected in this sentence. It is postponed until it costs nothing.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a retelling addressed to a community that was itself being asked for difficult things. The Quran gives the episode without dating it or naming the people in the land beyond the single word used for them. What the surah wants from the story is its shape, so the details a chronicle would supply are left out, and the reply is quoted at length instead.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to compel, or to set a broken bone by force. The word can describe a giant, a tyrant, or simply one who imposes, and the commentators note that all three senses were heard here.
The particle that carries the whole refusal. Everything before it is agreement and everything after it is a condition, which is how a postponement is made to sound very much like consent.

A participle rather than a verb, so it states a settled state instead of an act. Choosing this form for a promise about the future makes it sound far more certain than the speakers' behaviour warrants.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Every fortified settlement in the region was defended by people who had held it for generations and knew every approach to it. An attacking force fought uphill against walls, with no supply line behind them. The reluctance this passage records was militarily reasonable, and the audience hearing it in the city knew what that reasoning felt like from the inside, having faced decisions of the same shape.
studies.didYouKnow: The refusal in this ayah is quoted at greater length than the instruction that provoked it, and a second, blunter refusal is quoted two ayat later. The Quran gives more words here to what the people said than to what the prophet said, which is unusual, and which turns the passage into a study of one particular kind of answer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies a failure that is not disbelief and is much harder to see. Everything the speakers say is technically consistent with faith; what is missing is willingness to act while the outcome is still uncertain. That locates the test in timing rather than in doctrine. It also shows that a promise from God does not remove risk from the person who has to move first, and the passage does not pretend otherwise.

crossReferences.why: Answers immediately with two men who accept the same facts and draw the opposite conclusion.
Describes another moment of hanging back when the going was hard, and what was said of it.
Records a group who withdrew while others thought about God, and quotes their reasoning back.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you agree with something in principle and attach a condition to it. Write the condition down. Then ask what would have to be true for it to be met, and whether you would still be needed at that point. Some conditions are prudence. Some are a way of saying no while sounding like yes.

studies.title: Go At Them By The Gate
studies.meaning: Two voices break the consensus, and the passage describes them oddly: two men of those who feared, whom God had favoured. The fear is not denied, it is stated and then set beside the advice. Their counsel is tactical rather than inspiring, go in by the gate, and once you are inside you will prevail, and only after that practical instruction do they name reliance on God. Courage here is presented as a plan plus a trust, in that order.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The commentators identify the two men from the earlier scriptural tradition and differ over the details they report, which is why the Quran's own account leaves them unnamed and marked only by their fear and by God's favour on them. The surah is addressing a community that had recently lived through its own moments of collective hesitation, and it keeps the account very short.

keyTerms.note: The commentators read the object of this fear in more than one way: fear of God, or fear of the people holding the land. The Arabic leaves it open, and the ayah carries either reading.

A single definite gate, not gates in general. The advice is concrete enough to be acted on, which is what distinguishes it from encouragement, and the commentators note the practicality without settling which gate.
From a root for overcoming in a contest. Stated as a participle rather than as a promise verb, so the outcome is described as a condition they will be in rather than as a guarantee issued to them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A walled town lived or died at its gate. Walls could not be taken by men on foot, but a gate could be rushed at the right hour, and every raid in that world was planned around one. Those who knew the timing of the gates, when they opened for water carriers and when the watch changed, were worth more than fighters. Advice about a gate was expert advice.
studies.didYouKnow: The passage names the two men only by an attribute and never gives their names, though the older tradition supplies them and the classical commentaries record what it says. The Quran does this frequently, keeping a figure anonymous while preserving their words exactly, which shifts attention from who was speaking to what was actually said.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Reliance on God is placed after the plan, not instead of it, and the ordering is the passage's argument. The two men do not claim the outcome is assured regardless; they name a specific action, predict what follows it, and only then locate the whole thing in trust. That keeps trust from becoming a substitute for judgement. And the note that they feared makes courage a thing done with fear rather than in its absence.

crossReferences.why: Pairs consultation and decision with reliance on God, arranged in the same order as here.
Instructs preparation of whatever force can be mustered, then turns to reliance in the next breath.
Shows Jacob giving practical instructions to his sons and then naming God as the one relied on.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you have been praying about and have not planned for. Give it twenty minutes today: write down the first concrete step, the gate. Keep praying about it. The two men in this passage did both, and the passage puts the practical half first without treating it as any less faithful.

studies.title: We Are Staying Right Here
studies.meaning: The second refusal drops the pretence. Never, as long as they are in it. Then comes a sentence the commentators treat as the low point of the whole exchange: you and your Lord go and fight, we are sitting here. The prophet's response is not anger but a statement of limits, I control only myself and my brother, followed by a request to be separated from the people. He does not argue any further. He hands the situation back.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The Quran preserves the words of the refusal without softening them, which the commentators note is unusual for a passage recounting an earlier community's failure. The surah is building a case about covenants abandoned, and this is its sharpest illustration. The response that follows is quoted just as exactly, so a reader gets both the insult and the answer in their original form.

keyTerms.note: A participle of sitting, and the Quran uses the same word elsewhere for those who stay behind when others go out. A physical posture became a standing term for withholding oneself.

The verb of ownership again, applied here to the self. It concedes that a prophet's authority does not extend to compelling anyone, which is a statement about the limits of the office rather than a complaint.
To draw a distinction between two things, from the root that gives the word for a criterion. The request is that a division be made, not that a punishment be sent down.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A leader in Arabia commanded by consent, not by right. A chief who called for a march and was refused had no mechanism to compel anyone; men simply stayed at their tents, and the matter was over. Standing in front of a group that had decided not to move was among the most exposed positions in that society, and everyone hearing this passage had either been in it or watched someone be.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for sitting used in this refusal reappears in the Quran for those who stayed behind from later expeditions, and in one passage it is set directly against those who strive. A term for a body position became, through that kind of usage, one of the text's standard words for a moral choice.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prophet's answer defines prophethood by what it cannot do. He can deliver, and he can decline to be counted with a refusal, and there the office ends. That protects a reader from two errors at once: expecting a messenger to compel belief, and blaming him for a community's choice. The request to be separated is also not a curse; it asks for a distinction, and what follows is a consequence rather than a punishment sent.

crossReferences.why: Describes those who were glad to sit behind, using the same root for their position.
Contrasts those who sit at home with those who strive, without condemning the seated outright.
States that a prophet cannot compel people into belief, which is the limit named here.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you have been carrying a decision that is not yours to make: a relative's choice, a colleague's work, a friend's direction. Say the sentence this passage models, that you have control only over yourself. Then act on the part that actually is yours, and let the rest be someone else's to answer for.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Forty Years Of Wandering
studies.meaning: The answer to the request is a consequence, and it is measured. The land is closed to them for forty years, during which they will wander without bearings. Nothing is destroyed and nobody is struck down; the generation that refused simply does not arrive. The last clause is addressed to the prophet, and it concerns grief: do not sorrow over them. That instruction is easy to miss and is the reason the passage ends where it does rather than with the sentence.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The forty years is stated in the Quran itself rather than inferred, and the commentators note the correspondence with the older scriptural account without dwelling on it. The surah places this outcome shortly after the covenant it recalled at its opening, so a reader meets a pledge, a refusal and a consequence within twenty ayat of one another, which is the argument the arrangement is making.

keyTerms.note: Not simply travelling without arriving, but losing one's bearings; the root gives the word for a trackless waste. The wandering is described as a state of the people rather than of the route.
A number the Quran uses for a period of full maturing, as for the age at which a person reaches their strength. Here the span is long enough for one generation to be replaced by another.
A verb of sorrow bordering on despair, stronger than ordinary sadness. Telling the prophet not to feel it acknowledges that he otherwise would, which is why the instruction is given at all.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Forty years in that world was effectively a lifetime of adult memory. A man who could recall a drought forty years back was the oldest voice at a gathering, and his account of it settled arguments. To be told that a generation would circle in open country until it was gone was to be told, in terms everyone could measure, that this particular set of people would never see what they had been offered.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran mentions a period of forty in only four places: twice for the nights of an appointment on the mountain, once for the age at which a person reaches full strength, and here. In each case the number marks a completion rather than a stretch of time, which is why the commentators read it as a generation rather than as arithmetic.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The consequence fits the refusal exactly. People who would not enter are given endless movement without arrival, which is what they chose, extended. That is a pattern the Quran uses often: outcomes shaped like the acts that produced them rather than imposed from outside. The final instruction about grief adds something else, that a messenger is not required to carry sorrow for a decision he argued against and lost.

crossReferences.why: Continues the same history and describes what the people asked for instead of what was offered.
Records Moses asking not to be held responsible for what the foolish among them did.
Asks the Prophet whether he would destroy himself with grief over those who turn away.

studies.applyIt: Think of a decision someone close to you made against your advice, which you are still carrying. You argued; they chose. The instruction here is not to stop caring but to stop grieving as though the outcome were yours. Put it down for one day, deliberately, and see whether anything you were holding up actually falls.

studies.title: Accepted From One Of Them
studies.meaning: The story is introduced as something to be recited in truth, which signals that a version of it is already in circulation. Two offerings; one accepted, one not; and no reason given for the difference. The one refused announces murder rather than asking why. The reply is a single sentence and it does not defend the speaker: God accepts from those who are conscious of Him. The entire quarrel is left resting on that one line, with nothing added to soften it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The Quran gives no names, no place and no period, and the commentators supply names from the older tradition while treating them as material outside the text. The story is placed here because the surah has just recounted a refusal and its consequence; it now goes back to the first human quarrel and shows the same mechanism at its origin, before communities or covenants existed at all.

keyTerms.note: Built on the root for nearness. The word names what is offered by what it is for, so the thing given is defined by the approach it attempts rather than by any value of its own.
