studies.historicalContext: Medinan, within the passage about where allegiance belongs. The classical sources record reports of a specific occasion for this ayah, and the commentators do not agree about them, which is why the mainstream commentaries set out the accounts and the general reading together without ranking either. The setting on any reading is a community deciding whom to rely on while its alliances were unsettled.

keyTerms.note: The singular of the word used earlier for allies. Naming God first and in the singular makes protection one thing with a single source, which the rest of the sentence then extends rather than divides.
A participle describing the bowing posture of prayer, and in wider usage a bearing of humility. The commentators read the clause both ways, as a state the believers are in and as a particular act.
A group bound to one another by a common commitment. The Quran uses the word both of this alignment and of its opposite, so it names a kind of belonging rather than an honorific title.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man's patron was the most consequential fact about him. It determined who would avenge him, who would feed his family in a famine, and whether his word carried in a dispute. Changing patrons was possible and public, and the whole town knew when it happened. To be told that protection now ran through one source, and through the people who prayed and gave, was to be told the map had been redrawn.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase translated as the party of God appears twice in the Quran, both times as the closing clause of a passage about allegiance and both times promising the same outcome. Its opposite, a party belonging to the adversary, appears once, in the same surah as the second of those two, which makes the pairing deliberate.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Protection is described as a single thing with an order inside it: God, then the Messenger, then the believers, which places human solidarity downstream of a divine relation rather than beside it. The two markers given, prayer and the purifying due, are the vertical and the horizontal, so belonging is identified by what a person does with God and with other people, not by descent or by a stated position.

crossReferences.why: Gives the negative instruction that this ayah answers, only a few ayat earlier.
Closes another passage on allegiance with the same phrase and the same promise.
Describes believing men and women as protectors of one another, with the same two markers.

studies.applyIt: Look at your week and count the hours you give to the two things this ayah names: standing in prayer, and putting money or effort where it helps someone. Do not judge the number. Just have it. Whatever it turns out to be, add fifteen minutes to the smaller of the two this week and leave the rest alone.

studies.title: Those Who Make It A Joke
studies.meaning: The instruction about allies returns with a different criterion. What is named is not a community but a behaviour: taking your religion as mockery and as amusement. The ayah is explicit that such people may be found among those given scripture before you and among those who reject faith, which places the category across both lines rather than along them. The closing clause makes it a matter of consciousness of God rather than of grievance.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The commentators connect this ayah and the one after it to people who ridiculed the call to prayer when it was raised in the city, imitating it and laughing; reports vary in their detail. The call was new, audible across the whole town, and unavoidable, which is what made it a natural target and what makes the passage specific rather than general.

keyTerms.note: A noun rather than a verb, so the religion is described as having been turned into a thing of a certain kind. The grammar reports a transformation rather than a single incident of laughter.

The word for children's play, used across the Quran for activity without purpose. Pairing it with mockery separates two failures: treating something as ridiculous, and treating it as merely unserious.

The same word as the earlier instruction, and its placement at the end of a long sentence is deliberate: the criterion arrives before the category it applies to, so behaviour is what determines the outcome.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mockery was a weapon in Arabia, and a professional one. Poets were hired to satirise a rival tribe, and their verses travelled further and lasted longer than any raid. A community could be defended against attack and still be ruined by ridicule, because reputation determined who would trade, marry and ally with it. Taking mockery seriously was not thin skin; it was an accurate reading of that society.
studies.didYouKnow: The two words paired here, mockery and play, occur together again in the very next ayah, applied there to the call to prayer. The Quran often repeats a phrase across consecutive ayat this way, first as a criterion and then as the instance that illustrates it, and the pair appears nowhere else in the text.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The criterion given is behaviour, and it is explicitly said to cut across communities rather than to follow them. That is the passage's structural claim, and it matches the surah's practice elsewhere of naming conduct rather than groups. Ending on consciousness of God rather than on the offence also redirects the instruction inward: the guard asked for is over one's own alignment, not over anyone else's speech.

crossReferences.why: Gives the specific instance, mockery of the call to prayer, in the very next sentence.
Instructs withdrawal from a gathering where God's signs are ridiculed, until the subject changes.
Says to turn away from those who mock the signs until they enter some other discourse.

studies.applyIt: Notice which rooms you go quiet in. Everyone has one where their practice would be treated as a joke, and everyone manages it somehow. You do not have to leave the room. But this week, in one such conversation, say the ordinary true thing once, without defending it, and see what actually happens.

studies.title: When You Call To Prayer
studies.meaning: The general criterion becomes a specific scene. When you call to the prayer, they take it as mockery and as play. The verb and the nouns are the same as the ayah before, so criterion and instance are matched word for word. Then a reason is given, and it is unexpected: because they are a people who do not use reason. Ridicule is diagnosed as a failure of understanding rather than as hostility, which is a gentler judgement than the tone suggests.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The call to prayer was established in the city and was audible everywhere, which was the point of it. The commentators report that some who heard it imitated and laughed at it, and the reports differ over which individuals were involved. A public, repeated, unignorable summons was a new thing in that town, and reactions to it were part of how the community's presence was negotiated.

keyTerms.note: The verb of calling across a distance to someone who may not be looking your way. It suits a summons meant to reach people at work in their houses and fields, which is what the call was for.
From a root meaning to tie or tether, as a camel is hobbled. Reasoning in Arabic is a binding of things together, so the failure named is one of connection rather than of intelligence.

The word for aimless activity, repeated from the previous ayah. Its return in the same phrase joins the criterion to its instance, so the general rule and the particular case are linked by vocabulary.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Before the call was established, gathering people for prayer was a practical problem. The community discussed using a horn, a bell, or a fire lit on a height, and settled on a human voice from a rooftop. That choice made the summons unmistakably a person speaking rather than an instrument sounding, and it meant the words themselves, not just the signal, carried across the town.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran mentions the call to prayer in only two places: here, and in the short surah about the Friday gathering. That is a very small textual footprint for something so audible, and the classical sources discuss the call's establishment as a decision arrived at through consultation rather than as a matter settled in the text.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Attaching mockery to a failure of reasoning rather than to malice changes what the passage asks of a believer. If ridicule proceeds from not connecting things, then neither retaliation nor grievance is the indicated response. The ayah also treats the call as a test of the hearer rather than of the caller, which quietly relocates the whole situation: what is being measured is the reaction, not the summons itself.

crossReferences.why: Mentions the call to prayer again, in the passage about the Friday gathering.
Sets the criterion that this ayah illustrates, using the identical pair of words.
Describes hearts that do not reason, using the same verb for the failure named here.

studies.applyIt: The next time you hear the call, whether from a speaker, a phone, or your own memory of the hour, stop what you are doing for the length of it and listen to the words rather than treating it as a timer. It takes under a minute. Most of us have heard it thousands of times and never once listened.

studies.title: Do You Resent Us For This
studies.meaning: A question is put in the Prophet's mouth and it is close to disarming. Do you resent us for anything other than that we believe in God, and in what was sent down to us, and in what was sent down before? The list is the point: what is being objected to includes belief in their own scripture. The final clause is sharper, but the argument has already been made by the shape of the question rather than by what follows it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, addressed to communities of earlier scripture in the city. The commentators do not tie it to one exchange. The setting is a series of arguments in which the new community's claims were being contested, and the ayah's method is characteristic of this surah: it summarises the opponent's position back to them in the mildest possible terms and lets that summary do the work.

keyTerms.note: A verb for disapproval that leads toward retaliation, not mere dislike. It names finding fault with something and wanting it punished, which is why the mildness of the list that follows is so pointed.
The clause that makes the question work. It states that the belief being objected to includes their own revelation, so the objection turns out to be to an agreement rather than to a difference.
The same word used to close the earlier passage about judging by what was sent down. Its return here links the resentment described to the failure diagnosed only a few ayat before.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Argument in that world was conducted in public and remembered afterwards. Disputes between communities were carried on at gatherings and in markets, and a well-formed question repeated by bystanders could settle a matter more effectively than an answer. Rhetorical skill was not decoration; it was the mechanism by which positions actually moved, and this ayah's method would have been recognised at once.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb translated here as resent occurs only three times in the Quran, and in one of them it describes people who found fault with others for nothing except that they believed in God. The word carries the sense of taking revenge, so what it names is never merely a difference of opinion between parties.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates the disagreement precisely and then shows how small it is at the point of contact. What is objected to is belief in God and in revelation, including revelation the objectors accept. That framing does not resolve the dispute, but it changes what the dispute is about, and the surah has been doing this throughout: moving arguments from identity onto conduct and content.

crossReferences.why: Describes people persecuted for nothing except that they believed in God, using the same verb.
States belief in what was sent to earlier prophets without distinguishing between any of them.
Repeats the same declaration of belief across every revelation it names in turn.

studies.applyIt: In your next disagreement, try stating the other person's objection back to them in the plainest words you can find, and then stop. Do not add your answer. Half the time they will correct you, which means you had it wrong. The other half, hearing it said flatly does more than any argument you had prepared.

studies.title: Worse Than That In Recompense
studies.meaning: The question of the previous ayah is answered with a counter-question about recompense rather than about people. Shall I tell you of something worse in its outcome with God? What follows is a list of conditions: being cursed, incurring anger, the transformation the earlier scripture reports of a community that transgressed, and the service of false powers. The classical commentators differ over whether the transformation was of form or of state, and record both readings without deciding.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, answering an objection raised against the community. The episode alluded to belongs to the earlier scriptural history, and the Quran refers to it in two other places without narrating it fully. The commentators are careful to treat it as an account of a specific past group, since this surah's whole method is to name conduct and its consequences rather than to characterise any living community.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to come back, the same family as the word for a reward. Applied to a bad outcome, it keeps the sense of something returning to its origin rather than being imposed from outside.
From a root meaning to exceed all bounds, as floodwater does. The word names any authority that has overflowed its proper place, which is why it can cover idols, tyrants and systems alike.
A comparative from the verb to lose one's way. The passage measures distance from a road rather than depth of guilt, which keeps the image spatial and matches the sentence's closing phrase exactly.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Stories of communities destroyed for transgression were the common inheritance of the region, told at gatherings and along the trade routes. Ruined settlements in northern Arabia were pointed out to travellers as the remains of peoples who had been warned and had not listened. Such accounts were not exotic to this audience; they were part of the landscape, and they set the register for hearing a list like this.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran refers to this transformation in three places and never narrates it as a scene. In each case it is mentioned in a single clause inside a larger argument, which is unusual for the text's handling of dramatic events, and the classical commentaries note that restraint and generally read it as deliberate.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The answer given to an objection about a community is a list of conditions rather than a list of people. What is described is a trajectory: cursing, anger, transformation, and finally the service of what has overstepped its bounds. Placing that last makes it the destination rather than the starting point, so the passage reads as a warning about direction, which is how the classical commentaries generally handle it.

crossReferences.why: Refers to the same episode in a single clause, within the earlier Medinan surah.
Refers to it again, attached to an account of transgression concerning the sabbath.
Names the same false power, and sets rejection of it against holding fast to God.

studies.applyIt: Identify one thing you serve that has quietly outgrown its place: a metric at work, a schedule, an opinion you need from someone. Not evil, just oversized. Name it out loud, and then do one small thing this week that would be unthinkable if it were really in charge. That is the whole test the word here proposes.

studies.title: They Came In And Went Out
studies.meaning: A short sentence with a symmetry inside it. When they come to you they say we believe, and they entered with rejection and left with it. The two verbs bracket the visit, so the declaration made in the middle is surrounded on both sides by what did not change. Nothing is inferred about them; the passage states what was carried in and out. The closing clause then moves the whole matter to God's knowledge of what is concealed.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the section on people who presented one position and held another. The commentators tie the description to particular visitors in the city without agreeing on which, and read the ayah as describing a posture rather than naming a group. The setting is a town where formal visits between communities were frequent and where what was said at them was reported back and weighed.

keyTerms.note: Paired in this sentence with the verb for leaving, and both take the same object. The symmetry makes the visit a container: something was brought in and the same thing was carried out again.
To keep back something that others have a claim on, used in the Quran of withheld testimony and hidden scripture. It names suppression of what should be disclosed rather than ordinary privacy.

A comparative form used of God across the Quran. It does not merely assert knowledge but places it above the knowledge of everyone in the sentence, including the people being described about themselves.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Delegations were how business between communities was done. A group arrived, greetings were exchanged in fixed forms, positions were stated, and everyone went home to report. The formality was protective: it let two parties who did not trust each other meet without incident. It also meant that what was said in the meeting was understood by everyone present to be a performance as much as a disclosure.
studies.didYouKnow: The sentence uses two ordinary verbs of motion, entering and leaving, to frame an entire inner condition, and both take the same object. The Quran often works this way, carrying a judgement through the arrangement of very common words rather than through vocabulary that announces itself as religious.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage declines to accuse and instead describes a shape, then hands the assessment to God. That is a consistent move across this section: conduct is stated plainly and the verdict is withheld from the reader. It also names concealment as the real subject, which implies the visit itself was not the failure. What was hidden during it was, and only one party to the meeting could know that.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same distance between what is said aloud and what the heart holds.
States that God will call to account for what is in the hearts, whether shown or hidden.
Describes people saying with their mouths what was not in their hearts, on a particular day.

studies.applyIt: Think about a meeting you have coming up where you already know what you will say and what you will not. That is normal. But check one thing before you go: whether anything you are withholding is something the other person has a right to know. If it is, decide about it now, not in the room.

studies.title: Racing In Sin
studies.meaning: A single sentence of observation, and its verb is the striking part. You see many of them hurrying into wrongdoing, hostility, and the consuming of illicit gain. Hurrying is the same verb used a few ayat earlier of those rushing toward alliances out of fear, so the surah applies one word to two very different failures. The closing clause is a formula of dismay rather than a sentence passed: how wretched what they have been doing.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The passage sits in a stretch describing the conduct of some among the communities of earlier scripture, and the commentators note that the wording is careful: many of them, not all, which the surah has already qualified twice in similar descriptions. The setting is a market town where lending at interest, bribery in disputes and sharp practice in weights were all present and all profitable.

keyTerms.note: A form implying eagerness and competition, used elsewhere in the Quran of racing toward forgiveness. The same verb serves for hastening toward good and toward harm, so what it measures is appetite rather than direction.
From a root meaning to scrape away or to destroy utterly. The word occurs three times in the Quran and all three are in this surah, which is one way the chapter marks out its subject.
From the verb to cross a boundary. Paired with the general word for wrongdoing, it separates the wrong done in private from the wrong that reaches across and takes something from someone else.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A market in that world had no inspector. Weights were the trader's own, a debt could be rolled over with an addition each time, and a judge's favour could be secured with a gift that nobody called a bribe. None of it was hidden; it was simply how business ran for those who could get away with it. Everyone knew which houses had grown wealthy that way.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for illicit earnings appears three times in the Quran, all of them in this surah and within about twenty ayat of one another. Such concentration is rare, and the classical commentators treat repeated vocabulary of that kind as one of the ways a chapter signals what it is actually about.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The verb chosen is the passage's argument. Wrongdoing is not described here as weakness or as a slip but as eagerness, something people move toward quickly and competitively. That makes it a matter of appetite rather than of temptation resisted and lost. Using the same verb elsewhere for racing toward forgiveness implies the energy itself is neutral, and only its object decides what it becomes.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb for hurrying toward forgiveness and a garden, pointing that energy the other way.
Asks immediately why the scholars among them do not restrain exactly this behaviour.
Names consuming others' property wrongly, and using the authorities in order to do it.

studies.applyIt: Watch your own speed this week. There is something you get to quickly and something you approach slowly, and the gap between them tells you more than any list of intentions. Pick the one you are slow to and start it ten minutes earlier once. Speed is habit, and habit is what this ayah is measuring.

studies.title: Why Do They Not Restrain Them
studies.meaning: The question turns from those doing wrong to those who watch them do it. Why do the teachers and the scholars not restrain them from their sinful speech and their consuming of illicit gain? The closing formula is the same one used of the wrongdoers in the previous ayah, with a single verb changed. The commentators notice the change: the doers were described by what they do, and the scholars by what they produce, which is the harsher of the two.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following directly on the description of wrongdoing in the preceding ayah and read with it by the commentators as one unit. The setting is a city where scholars held real authority: they gave rulings, settled disputes and taught, and their silence on a practice functioned as permission. The passage addresses that authority rather than the practice, which is the shift the two ayat perform together.

keyTerms.note: A particle that both asks a question and expresses reproach. It is not a neutral enquiry; the form already contains the judgement, which is why the ayah needs no accusation after it.
The verb of forbidding, but its root sense is reaching a limit. What is asked for is the placing of an end point, which in a society without enforcement was largely a matter of speech.
A verb of craft and deliberate production, replacing the plainer verb for doing used one ayah earlier. The change makes the scholars' silence a thing constructed rather than merely a thing done.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A scholar's word travelled. He was consulted at weddings and funerals, at the settling of estates and the drawing of contracts, and what he declined to object to was recorded by everyone present as acceptable. His household was supported by the community he advised, which meant that objecting to a wealthy family's practice carried a direct cost. The passage names that pressure without excusing it.
studies.didYouKnow: The two ayat end with formulas differing by a single word: one uses the ordinary verb for doing, the other a verb meaning to craft or fabricate. Classical commentators reading the pair together generally take the second as the graver, on the grounds that silence in the face of a wrong is something a person builds rather than something that happens to them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Responsibility is extended from the act to the surrounding permission. The passage does not accuse the scholars of doing the wrong; it accuses them of not placing a limit on it, and it treats that omission as a form of production. That is a claim about how communities decay: not through the number of wrongdoers but through the number of people who decide that saying something is not their part.

crossReferences.why: Describes an earlier community that did not restrain one another from the wrongs they committed.
Names the practices this question is about, in the ayah immediately before it.
Describes a community defined by enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong.

studies.applyIt: Think of a thing said or done regularly around you that you have decided not to object to. You have reasons, and they are probably good ones. This week, in one instance, say the smallest possible version of the objection: not a speech, one sentence, without heat. Notice whether anything you feared actually follows.

studies.title: His Hands Are Outstretched
studies.meaning: A saying is quoted and answered in the same breath. Someone said that God's hand is tied, and the reply reverses it word for word: their own hands are tied. Then the correction. Rather, both His hands are outstretched, and He spends as He wills. The image of two open hands is among the most striking figures in the Quran, and the commentators handle it as they handle all such expressions, affirming the generosity it conveys without picturing a form.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical commentators attribute the saying to particular individuals rather than to a whole community, and the reports about who said it and in what circumstance differ from one another. The wider setting is a period of hardship in which such a remark, about God's provision having been withdrawn, would have had an obvious occasion. The ayah answers the theology rather than pursuing the speakers.

keyTerms.note: A passive participle used of a hand chained to the neck, an image the Quran employs elsewhere for miserliness. The saying accuses God of the very thing this word ordinarily accuses a human being of.

A dual form, so two hands specifically. The commentators read the dual as intensifying generosity rather than describing a body, since Arabic uses open hands for giving as naturally as English uses an open door.
The verb of putting out a fire, used here of a war that has been kindled. It describes not a battle won but a fire that fails to take, which is a quieter kind of intervention than victory.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A closed fist and an open hand were the standard Arabian gestures for meanness and generosity, and the poets used them constantly. A chief was praised as one whose palm was never closed, and stinginess was described as a hand bound to the neck. The saying quoted here was not abstract theology; it borrowed the most ordinary insult in the language and pointed it upward.
studies.didYouKnow: The same image of a hand chained to the neck appears in another surah as advice to a person about their own spending, warning against both the closed fist and the hand opened until nothing remains. The Quran therefore uses one gesture for human balance and, in the dual, for a divine generosity that has no ceiling.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply does not argue that God is generous; it performs the reversal grammatically, turning the accusation back on the accusers before making any claim at all. Then it states the positive in the widest possible terms: He spends as He wills. The passage also shows how the tradition reads figurative language about God, affirming what the image conveys while refusing to convert it into a description of form.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same image of a hand tied to the neck, as advice about a person's own spending.
Records another saying attributed to some, that God is poor and that they are rich.
Says that God withholds and gives in abundance, and that to Him is the return.

studies.applyIt: Notice how you talk about your own resources when you are anxious. There is a way of saying we cannot afford it that is accurate, and a way that is a small theology. Say one true, specific sentence about your situation this week instead of the general one. The general one is usually where the tied hand creeps in.

studies.title: Had They Believed
studies.meaning: A conditional sentence, and the whole force lies in its mood. Had the people of the scripture believed and been conscious of God, We would have covered over their wrongs and admitted them to gardens of delight. Nothing is denied to them and nothing is promised; a door is described as open and not walked through. Coming immediately after a long stretch of criticism, the shift is abrupt, and the commentators note that the surah repeatedly interrupts itself this way.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, placed directly after some of the surah's sharpest material about conduct. The commentators read the sudden turn as characteristic of the chapter: criticism is followed by an opening rather than by a conclusion. No specific occasion is reported. The people addressed were neighbours in the city with whom the community traded, argued and shared a street, and not an abstraction at a distance.

keyTerms.note: From the root for covering, the same used earlier in this surah for atonement. Wrongs are described as buried rather than as never committed, which keeps the record honest while removing its weight.
From the verb to guard oneself. Paired here with believing, it names an ongoing wariness rather than a single act of assent, so the condition described is a way of living rather than a declaration.
An intensive noun from the root for a soft and pleasant life. Attaching it to gardens describes the quality of the place rather than its features, which is unusual in the Quran's garden imagery.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A garden in Arabia was a walled enclosure with running water and shade, the most valuable property a family could hold and the clearest picture of ease that anyone had. Owning one meant no longer worrying about the season. When the Quran uses the word, the audience heard a specific and coveted thing, not a symbol: the difference between a life of calculation and a life of enough.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and the one after it are both built as unfulfilled conditionals, describing what would have followed from something that did not happen. The Quran uses that construction sparingly, and here it produces two consecutive sentences of a kind that criticise and invite at the same time without doing either of them directly.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage keeps the future open while describing the past honestly. Nothing in it forecloses anything, and the criticism that precedes it is neither withdrawn nor allowed to settle into a verdict. That combination is a recurring shape in this surah, and it says something about how the Quran wants disagreement held: descriptions of conduct are final, descriptions of people are not.

crossReferences.why: Continues with a second conditional, about what upholding their scriptures would have produced.
Ends a similar passage of correction with an invitation rather than with a conclusion.
Names a standing community among them who recite the signs of God through the night.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone you have quietly written off. Not an enemy, just a person you have concluded will not change. Say to yourself the sentence this ayah models: if they did, what would follow. Then behave for one week as though that were still available. The change, if there is one, will show in how you speak to them.

studies.title: Eating From Above And Below
studies.meaning: A second conditional follows the first, and this one concerns sustenance rather than the hereafter. Had they upheld the Torah and the Gospel and what was sent down to them, they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet. Rain and harvest, named as directions rather than as things. Then the sentence does something the surrounding criticism has not: it names a moderate community among them, before returning to the many.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The commentators read the phrase about above and below as rain from the sky and produce from the ground, the two sources of every livelihood in an agricultural society. The clause acknowledging a balanced group among them is noted in the classical commentaries as a deliberate qualification, and it matches similar acknowledgements elsewhere in this surah and in the surah before it.

keyTerms.note: The verb for making something stand, used across the Quran for establishing prayer. Applying it to a scripture means putting it into practice rather than merely possessing, preserving or reciting it.
From a root meaning to aim straight for something and to keep to the middle of a road. It names a group that neither exceeds nor falls short, and the same root gives the word for economy.
A direction rather than a substance. Pairing it with beneath the feet covers the two sources of food in that world, rain and soil, without naming either, which makes the promise total.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything in Arabia depended on two directions. Rain came or it did not, and the wells and the date palms answered accordingly. A year's whole prospect could be read in the sky within a fortnight, and villages sent watchers to high ground for the first clouds. To describe abundance as eating from above and below was to name every possible source at once, in the only terms that mattered.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause naming a balanced community among them is one of several places in this surah where a broad criticism is immediately narrowed. The chapter does this repeatedly, using words like many of them rather than all, and the classical commentaries treat those qualifications as binding on how the surrounding material should be read.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Sustenance is presented as tied to conduct, which the Quran does elsewhere and always with care: the claim is about a community over time rather than about an individual's fortune in a given year. What makes the ayah notable is the qualification. Having described a large failure, it stops to name those the description does not apply to, and the commentaries treat that clause as decisive.

crossReferences.why: Says belief and God-consciousness would have opened blessings from the sky and the earth.
Names a standing community among the people of scripture who are not like the rest.
Describes provision arriving from a direction the person had not reckoned on.

studies.applyIt: Look at where this month's provision actually came from. Not the salary line, the whole chain: the person who hired you, the rain that grew the food, the health that let you work. Write down three links you had no part in arranging. It takes five minutes and it changes what the word earning means.

studies.title: Convey What Was Sent Down
studies.meaning: A short instruction with the largest possible stake attached. Convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord; and if you do not, then you have not delivered His message. The conditional is absolute: partial delivery counts as none. Then a promise of protection follows, which tells you what the instruction was up against. The commentators record more than one account of the occasion and do not agree, setting the reports out without ranking them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources preserve several accounts of when this ayah was revealed and what it directly concerned, and they differ; the commentaries record the range rather than resolving it. What is agreed is the setting: a period in which delivering the message carried real physical risk, which is why the ayah pairs its instruction with an assurance of protection rather than with a warning.

keyTerms.note: From the verb to reach a destination, in a form meaning to make something arrive. What is asked is not speech but arrival, so the measure of success lies with the hearer rather than the speaker.
From a root meaning to hold something back from falling or from harm, the same family as the word for a bond or a firm grip. Protection is described as a holding rather than a covering over.
The word for a message sent and, by extension, for the office of the one who carries it. Using the singular makes the whole commission one thing, which is why leaving out a part fails all of it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A messenger in Arabia carried words he was not permitted to edit. Delegations memorised what they were sent with and recited it back verbatim, sometimes to hostile audiences, and a messenger who softened a message on arrival had failed at his only task. The convention protected the sender and endangered the carrier, and everyone in that society understood which of the two bore the risk.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for conveying gives its name to an entire discipline in Arabic, the study of how speech is shaped so that it arrives at its hearer. The same root also produces the word for reaching maturity, so the language treats delivery, arrival and coming of age as versions of a single idea.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction defines a messenger entirely by transmission and makes no allowance for judgement about what an audience can bear. That is a demanding standard, and the assurance of protection is attached to it rather than to the outcome, which suggests the risk was expected to be real and the reception uncertain. The passage also implies that revelation is a deposit rather than a possession.

crossReferences.why: States that nothing rests on the Messenger except the delivery of the message itself.
Describes those who deliver the messages of God and fear no one except Him.
Says the Messenger's charge is what was placed on him, and yours is what was placed on you.

studies.applyIt: There is something you have been asked to pass on and have been softening: a decision, a diagnosis, a colleague's honest view. Deliver it once this week in the words you were given, without your own cushioning. You can be kind about the manner. This ayah's whole subject is the difference between kindness and editing.

studies.title: You Stand On Nothing
studies.meaning: The instruction to convey is followed immediately by what is to be conveyed, and it is blunt. You stand on nothing until you uphold the Torah and the Gospel and what was sent down to you from your Lord. The demand is that they apply their own scriptures, not that they abandon them. Then the ayah concedes that the message will increase many of them in defiance, and closes by telling the Prophet not to grieve over that.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, addressed to communities holding earlier scripture. The commentators read it together with the ayah before it, taking the instruction to convey and this content as a single movement. No specific occasion is reported. The setting is the ongoing argument in the city about what each community's scripture required of it, in which this ayah takes a position that is demanding and generous at once.

keyTerms.note: Literally standing on no thing, an idiom for having no footing at all. The image is spatial: what is denied is a place to stand rather than a claim to be right, which is a sharper accusation.

The verb for making something stand, used across the Quran of establishing prayer. Applied to scripture it means putting the text into practice, and its choice here answers the image of having no footing.
From the root for water overflowing its banks. What increases is not disbelief alone but a spilling past limits, which the Quran treats as a failure distinct from denial itself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Standing was the posture of a claim. A man rose to speak in a dispute, and where he stood in the assembly signalled what backing he had behind him. To tell a group they were standing on nothing borrowed from that setting directly: not that their argument was weak, but that there was no ground under them at all, which was the most complete dismissal the idiom allowed.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about the revelation increasing many of them in defiance appears twice in this surah, in nearly identical words, four ayat apart. Repetition at that distance is one of the surah's structural habits, and the classical commentators generally read the second occurrence as closing a section that the first one opened.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The demand made of another community is that it be faithful to its own revelation, which sets the pattern for how this surah handles difference throughout. It also concedes something unusual: that the arrival of guidance can make some people worse. That is stated without embarrassment and followed by an instruction against grief, so the passage builds the failure of the message into the message's own account of itself.

crossReferences.why: Contains the same clause about the revelation increasing many of them in defiance.
Instructs the people of the Gospel to judge by what God sent down within it.
Says the revelation is healing for believers and increases only loss for wrongdoers.

studies.applyIt: Take the tradition you belong to and ask what it actually asks of you this week, in its plainest terms, rather than what you enjoy about belonging to it. Do one of those things on Thursday. This ayah's whole demand is for footing, and footing comes from practice rather than from possession.

studies.title: Nothing To Fear, No Grief
studies.meaning: Four communities are listed by name and then the sentence starts again with a condition that cuts across all of them: whoever believes in God and the Last Day and acts rightly. The commentators discuss the grammar closely, since the listing is taken over by a singular relative clause. What is promised is stated as an absence, no fear and no grief, which are the two directions anxiety runs, forward towards what may come and back over what is gone.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a late surah addressed largely to communities holding earlier scriptures, in a passage that has just told them their books do not stand on nothing. A near-identical sentence appears earlier in the Quran at 2:62. The commentators treat the repetition as deliberate, and note that the placement here follows an appeal rather than a rebuke.

keyTerms.note: A community named three times in the Quran and never described. Classical commentators offer differing identifications and several say plainly that the group is not certainly known, so the name is left standing as given.
Anxiety directed forward, at what has not yet happened. Across the Quran it is paired with a word for grief over what already has, and the two together cover the whole timeline of distress.
The verb for working, joined to a word meaning sound or fit for purpose. Right action is described as repair, making something work as it should, rather than as compliance with an instruction.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Religious identity in Arabia was inherited and public, tied to which shrines your people kept and which oaths they swore by. Communities lived side by side in Medina with their own courts, festivals and burial grounds, and a person's group was visible in their name. A sentence that named four communities and then made the same statement about individuals inside them worked against the grain of how everyone was categorised.
studies.didYouKnow: In this ayah the word for the Sabians stands in the nominative case, where the construction would normally require the accusative, as it does at 2:62. It is among the most discussed grammatical features in the Quran, and the classical grammarians explained it as a deliberate suspension that sets the word slightly apart from the list around it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The sentence puts the decisive weight on what a person believes and does rather than on the label they carry, without dissolving the labels: the communities are named, not merged. The promise is framed as removal rather than addition, which is a specific kind of comfort. It does not say what such people will be given. It says what will not be there, and names the whole of what human beings are usually afraid of.

crossReferences.why: States the same sentence with the communities in a different order and a reward clause added.
Gives the same promise to whoever submits and does good, in the singular.
Explains why the communities differ, and tells them to compete in good works.

studies.applyIt: Write down the fear that has been running underneath this week, and the regret that has been running alongside it. One sentence each. The ayah names those two and only those two, which suggests that almost everything heavy you are carrying is one or the other, and it helps just to see which.

studies.title: Whenever A Messenger Came
studies.meaning: A covenant is recalled and messengers are sent, and then a pattern is stated rather than a set of events. Whenever a messenger came with what their souls did not desire, one group they called liars and another they killed. The word whenever makes it a repeated shape rather than a list of incidents. The two responses are not treated identically, and the grammar keeps them apart: one is stated as completed, the other in a continuing form.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a section reviewing the history of covenants made and broken. The Quran does not name individual messengers or episodes here; it gives the pattern and leaves the instances to an audience that partly knew them. The commentators supply names from the earlier tradition while treating them as material alongside the text rather than as part of it.

keyTerms.note: A construction of repetition rather than of a single instance. It converts a set of events into a habit, which is why the ayah reads as the description of a mechanism rather than an accusation about particular occasions.

From the root for falling or inclining downward, the same word used for the desires the Prophet is warned against following. The criterion for rejection is named here as appetite rather than as evidence.

An imperfect verb where the previous clause used a past tense, so the killing is described as ongoing while the denial is complete. Classical grammarians read the shift as making the second response the more vivid.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man who told a tribe something it did not want to hear had two things to fear, and neither of them was argument. He could be discredited, which cost him his standing and his ability to trade or marry, or he could be dealt with more directly on a road somewhere. Both outcomes were common enough that anyone bringing unwelcome news calculated them in advance.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah shifts tense between its two clauses, describing the accusation of lying in the past and the killing in a continuing form. Classical grammarians treated such shifts as deliberate rather than loose, and the commentaries on this ayah discuss the change at length, generally reading it as bringing the second act before the listener's eyes.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The criterion for rejection is located in desire rather than in evidence, which is the passage's real claim. Messengers were not refused because their case was weak but because of what their message asked. That makes the pattern portable: any community can be measured by how it treats what it did not want to hear, and the surah has been building toward exactly this point.

crossReferences.why: States the same pattern in the earlier surah, naming the same two responses in order.
Continues with what they assumed would follow, and with what happened twice over.
Describes messengers sent one after another, each denied by the community he came to.

studies.applyIt: Recall the last time someone told you something true that you did not want to hear. Did you argue with the content or with the person? Most of us go for the person, because it is quicker. Find that conversation again, and go back to whatever the content actually was. It is probably still waiting.

studies.title: Blind And Deaf, Then Again
studies.meaning: A calculation is described and then its consequence. They reckoned there would be no reckoning, so they went blind and deaf. Then God turned toward them. Then many of them went blind and deaf again. The structure is the point: a failure, a mercy, and the same failure returning, with the mercy placed in the middle rather than at the end. The closing clause adds nothing except that God sees what they do.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the review of an earlier community's history. The Quran compresses centuries into a single sentence with three turns in it, which the commentators note is characteristic of the way this surah handles the past: not as chronicle but as pattern. No specific episodes are named, and the classical commentaries fill them in from the older tradition where they can.

keyTerms.note: The verb of accounting and arithmetic, used for forming an expectation. It shares a root with the word for the final reckoning, so the sentence has them miscalculating the very thing they are calculating about.

Two verbs in a form describing something that happened to them, not a condition they were born with. The commentators read the pair as a loss of perception that follows a choice rather than preceding it.

The same verb used for a person's own repentance, with a preposition that reverses its direction. Placing it in the middle of the sentence makes mercy an event within the history rather than its conclusion.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Blindness and deafness were common and carried real consequences. A man who could not see could not travel alone or judge a beast at market; a man who could not hear was cut out of the poetry and the news that were the entire information system of a tribe. Using the two together named a person removed from every means by which anyone learned anything.
studies.didYouKnow: The two verbs for blindness and deafness appear in the same order twice within this single ayah, with a sentence of mercy standing between them. That kind of exact repetition inside one ayah is uncommon in the Quran, and it makes the shape of the sentence carry the argument before any of its words do.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing God's turning in the middle of the sentence rather than at its close says something about how the passage understands mercy: it is not the resolution of a history but an event inside one, and it can be followed by the same failure again. That is a sober picture, and it refuses two easy readings at once, that a community is finished, and that having been forgiven settles anything.

crossReferences.why: Describes hearts hardening after signs were shown, in a review of the same history.
Gives the pattern of rejection that this ayah says they assumed would carry no consequence.
Describes those God has made deaf and whose sight He has blinded, after turning away.

studies.applyIt: Think of a change you made after something went wrong, and then let slip back. Not a failure of resolve; almost everyone's list is long. Pick one and restart it today rather than waiting for the next thing to go wrong. This ayah's whole shape is about the stretch that comes after relief arrives.

studies.title: Worship God, My Lord And Yours
studies.meaning: A claim is named and then answered by quoting the one it is made about. The Messiah himself said: children of Israel, worship God, my Lord and your Lord. Setting his own words against the claim is the whole argument, and the first possessive is doing the work, since my Lord makes him one of the worshippers. What follows states the consequence of associating others with God, and it is given in the Messiah's reported speech rather than in the Quran's own voice.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the surah's address to Christian communities. Such communities were present across the peninsula and delegations reached the city, so the passage had actual interlocutors. The commentators do not attach it to a single meeting. The formulation being addressed is specific, and the Quran is careful through this section to name a proposition rather than to characterise everyone who might hold something like it.

keyTerms.note: The first possessive is what carries the argument. By naming God as his own Lord, the reported speech places the speaker inside the same relation as his listeners rather than anywhere above it.

From the root for sharing or partnership, as in a commercial venture. The word describes giving something a share in what belongs to God alone, which is why the commentators treat it as a matter of attribution.
A place one comes back to for shelter. Using the word for refuge of the fire is deliberate and bleak: what should be a return to safety turns out to be the destination itself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reported speech was how authority worked in that world. A claim was strong or weak according to whose words stood behind it, and a saying attributed to a respected figure could end an argument outright. Chains of transmission were tracked carefully in poetry and genealogy long before they were used for anything else. Answering a claim about someone with that person's own words was the strongest available move.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah contains the longest reported exchange between God and Jesus anywhere in the Quran, near its very end, and every quotation of his speech in the chapter places him as a servant addressing God or as a messenger addressing his own people. He is never quoted here speaking about himself in the third person.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument is made by attribution rather than by assertion. Instead of denying a claim outright, the ayah sets it beside words reported from the figure it concerns and lets the two stand together. That method respects the sources of the community being addressed while making the contradiction plain, and it recurs across this whole section of the surah.

crossReferences.why: Gives Jesus saying he told them only what he was commanded, to worship God his Lord and theirs.
Reports the same statement, that God is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him.
Reports it once more, within the account of his call to his own people.

studies.applyIt: When you next want to know what someone thinks, go to what they actually said rather than to what is said about them. It takes longer and it is nearly always different. This ayah's whole method is to set a claim beside a quotation, and most disagreements you are in would not survive ten minutes of that.

studies.title: Will They Not Turn Back
studies.meaning: A formulation is named and denied, and then something unexpected follows. There is no god but one God; and if they do not stop saying it, a painful punishment will reach those among them who reject. The qualification is careful, those among them, not all of them. And then the very next sentence is not a threat but a question. Will they not turn to God and seek His forgiveness. The passage moves from denial to invitation in a single step.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, addressing a specific theological formulation rather than a community. The commentators discuss what exactly is being denied and are careful to state the proposition precisely. The setting is the same series of encounters with Christian communities in and around the city. The passage's sudden turn toward invitation in the second ayah is noted in the classical commentaries as its most characteristic feature.

keyTerms.note: A construction meaning one of a set of three. The commentators note that the Arabic names a counting rather than a relation, which is why they discuss so carefully what proposition is being reported and denied.

From the root for reaching a limit, the same used earlier in the surah for scholars restraining others. Here it is intransitive: reaching one's own limit and stopping, which is a description of turning back.

A question with a particle of gentle reproach rather than accusation. Placing it directly after a warning changes the register entirely, and the sentence that follows names God as forgiving and merciful.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Theological argument arrived in Arabia along the trade roads, and it arrived unsettled. The churches of Syria, Egypt and Abyssinia disagreed with one another in ways that traders repeated without fully following, and formulations that had taken councils to produce were summarised in a sentence by the time they reached a market in the peninsula. The Quran engages the formulation it names with precision.
studies.didYouKnow: The second of these two ayat is one of the shortest in the surah and consists almost entirely of a question. The Quran frequently follows a severe statement with a short opening of exactly this kind, and the brevity is part of the effect: nothing is added to the invitation, and no condition at all is attached to it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage denies a proposition, names a consequence, and then immediately offers a way out, all within two sentences. The order matters: the invitation comes after the warning rather than instead of it, so neither one cancels the other. It also names God as forgiving and merciful at the exact point where a reader expects the argument to close, which is how this surah repeatedly ends its hardest passages.

crossReferences.why: Addresses the same formulation and closes with an instruction to say what is better for you.
Names the related claim and answers it with the Messiah's own reported words.
Tells those who exceeded against themselves not to despair of the mercy of God.

studies.applyIt: Notice how you end an argument you believe you have won. Most of us stop at the point of being right. This passage does not: it states the disagreement and then leaves a door open in the next breath. In your next disagreement, say the door sentence out loud, whatever yours is, before you walk away.

studies.title: They Both Ate Food
studies.meaning: The argument is made with the plainest possible fact. The Messiah, son of Mary, was only a messenger; messengers had passed before him; and his mother was a woman of complete truthfulness. Then the sentence everyone remembers: they both used to eat food. Nothing about doctrine, nothing about miracles. A daily necessity is named, and the necessity is the argument. The ayah closes by pointing at the clarity of the signs and the strangeness of what is done with them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the address to Christian communities in and around the city. No specific occasion is reported for it. The Quran's method through this section is to argue from what both parties already accept, and the choice of eating as the point of contact reflects that: it is the one thing nobody disputes, and it requires no scripture at all to establish.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form from the root for truth, used in the Quran of a small number of figures. It names someone whose truthfulness is constitutional rather than occasional, and it is the highest description the text gives her.
The verb for a place becoming empty or a stretch of time going by. Applied to the messengers before him, it says only that they came and were gone, which is exactly the point being made.
A dual verb in a continuous form, so habitually and both of them. The grammar insists on the ordinariness: not that they once ate, but that eating was a regular feature of their lives.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Food was the marker of creatureliness in that world's thinking. Idols were mocked in the Quran for not eating, and stories of extraordinary beings usually had them needing nothing at all. Everyone knew what depending on a meal meant: a body that weakens, a household that must provide, a season that can fail. Naming eating was the shortest route to placing someone within the created order.
studies.didYouKnow: Mary is the only woman named in the Quran, and the description given her here, a woman of complete truthfulness, is applied elsewhere in the text to a prophet. It ranks her by a quality of character rather than by a role, which is the pattern the Quran generally keeps to when it describes her.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage argues from the body. Whatever is claimed about a person, a person who requires food depends on something outside themselves, and the ayah lets that do all the work. It also honours Mary in the same breath as it makes the argument, which is characteristic: the correction of a claim about her son is not permitted to diminish her, and both moves happen in one sentence.

crossReferences.why: Says the messengers sent before all ate food and walked about in the markets.
States that they were not bodies which did not eat, nor were they immortal.
Describes Mary as chosen and purified above the women of all the worlds.

studies.applyIt: Eat one meal this week slowly, with your attention on the fact of needing it. Not gratitude exactly; just the plain observation that you stop working without this, several times a day, for your whole life. This ayah builds an argument out of that fact, and the fact is available to you three times daily.

studies.title: Neither Harm Nor Benefit
studies.meaning: Two questions and then an instruction. The first asks whether people worship, besides God, what has no power to harm or benefit them, and the test offered is capability rather than doctrine. The second addresses the people of scripture directly: do not go to excess in your religion beyond the truth, and do not follow the inclinations of a people who went astray earlier and led many others astray. Excess, not deficiency, is what gets named as the danger.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the surah's long address to communities of earlier scripture. The commentators read the warning against excess as directed at a specific pattern rather than at devotion in general: the raising of a figure beyond what was ever claimed for him. No particular occasion is reported for either ayah, and the passage sits at the end of the section as its summary.

keyTerms.note: The standard pair the Quran uses to test a claim to power. Naming harm first is deliberate: something that cannot even hurt you has no leverage at all, which is a lower bar than being unable to help.
From a verb meaning to boil over, also used of prices rising past what a thing is worth. The image is of something exceeding its measure, so what is warned against is inflation rather than intensity.

The same word used earlier in this surah for what a judge is warned against following. Its return here places doctrinal excess and judicial pressure under one description, as things wanted rather than things concluded.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia was full of powers that could not act. Stones at shrines were consulted about journeys and marriages, offerings were left at them, and their reputations rose and fell with events nobody could connect to them. The question about harm and benefit was not a philosophical exercise for that audience; it named the practical uselessness of things their own families had relied on.
studies.didYouKnow: The warning against excess in religion appears twice in the Quran, in this surah and in the surah before it, both times addressed to the people of scripture and both times in almost identical words. It is one of very few instructions in the text that guard against going too far rather than against not going far enough.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies a failure that devotion produces on its own. Nothing here concerns neglect; the danger named is enthusiasm running past what is true, and the Quran treats that as a way of losing a religion rather than of intensifying it. Pairing it with the question about harm and benefit is pointed: excess and idolatry are placed in one sentence as two ways of misplacing power.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same warning against excess in religion, in almost exactly identical words.
Describes worshipping besides God what neither harms nor benefits, using the same test.
Makes a parallel argument about the Messiah from an entirely ordinary human need.

studies.applyIt: Look at a practice you are proud of, and ask whether any part of it has grown past what it was for: a rule you added, a strictness nobody asked for, a hill you now defend. Trim one inch off it this week. Excess is the harder failure to see, because it looks exactly like commitment.

studies.title: They Did Not Restrain One Another
studies.meaning: A curse is reported as having come through the tongues of two prophets, and then the reason is given in the next sentence, which is the passage's whole point. They did not restrain one another from the wrongdoing they were committing. Not that they did wrong, which is stated separately, but that they let it stand among them. The closing formula repeats the one used earlier in this surah for scholars who kept silent.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a review of an earlier community's history. The Quran names David and Jesus as the tongues through which the curse came, and does not describe the episodes at all; the commentators supply accounts from the older tradition. Placing this immediately after a long section on conduct within the community being addressed suggests, as the classical commentaries note, that the warning was not meant to stay in the past.

keyTerms.note: An idiom for something spoken through someone rather than by them. It keeps the words as God's while identifying the human voice that carried them, which is how the Quran often describes prophetic speech.

A reciprocal form, so the restraining runs in every direction rather than downward from an authority. What is described as missing is mutual correction among equals, not the enforcement of a rule from above.
From the verb to not recognise. A wrong is named as something a healthy community fails to recognise as its own, so the word already contains the reaction the passage says was missing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A tribe policed itself through speech. There were no officers, so a man was restrained by knowing that an uncle or a neighbour would say something at the next gathering and that the remark would be remembered. When that stopped happening, nothing else took its place. Everyone in the audience had watched a family let something go and had seen how quickly the next thing followed.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for restraining one another is reciprocal in form, which is unusual for this root in the Quran. Elsewhere the forbidding of wrong is generally described as something a person or a community does to others; the reciprocal form makes it something a group owes to itself in every direction at once.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Guilt is distributed by the passage rather than concentrated. The wrongdoing is named once and the silence around it is named separately and given a whole ayah, which places the two on comparable footing. That is a claim about how a community is judged: not by its worst members but by what the rest of it tolerated, and the surah has already applied the same measure to scholars.

crossReferences.why: Applies the same measure to scholars who did not restrain those around them.
Describes a community defined by enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong.
Warns of a trial that will not strike only those among you who did the wrong.

studies.applyIt: Think of a group you belong to that has one thing everyone privately dislikes and nobody names. You are probably waiting for someone better placed to say it. So is everyone else. Say the mildest possible version at the next opportunity, and notice how many people agree with you afterwards in private.

studies.title: What Their Souls Sent Ahead
studies.meaning: One sentence of observation and one of consequence. You see many of them turning for support to those who reject faith. Then a formula of dismay: how wretched is what their own souls have sent on ahead of them. The verb is the striking part, because it makes the alliance a shipment rather than a decision, something despatched forward to a destination. The closing clauses name what arrived there: God's displeasure, and a punishment they remain in.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the stretch describing conduct during a period of unsettled alliances. The commentators tie the description to particular individuals and are careful about the wording, which says many of them rather than all. The passage belongs to the same discussion as the earlier ayat on protection pacts, and the classical commentaries read the whole sequence together as one argument about allegiance.

keyTerms.note: The verb of sending something on ahead of you, as goods were despatched before a traveller set out. Deeds are pictured as freight already in transit, which makes the outcome an arrival rather than a sentence.
A word for displeasure stronger than the ordinary term, and the direct opposite of the word for good pleasure used earlier in this surah. The two frame the same relation from either end of it.

The self named as the agent, exactly as in the account of the first murder earlier in this surah. Both passages make the interior the actor, which keeps responsibility from being displaced outward onto anything else.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Merchants sent goods ahead of themselves. A caravan carried a man's consignment to a market he would reach weeks later, and by the time he arrived the goods were already there, already sold or already spoiled. Nothing could be recalled once it had left. The image behind this ayah's verb was a commercial routine every trading family understood in their bones.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses the language of sending something on ahead for deeds in a number of places, and it is one of the text's most persistent metaphors: the present is described as a place from which things are despatched, and the hereafter as the place where they are collected. The vocabulary is drawn entirely from trade.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Consequence is described as arrival rather than as verdict. Nothing in the sentence has God reacting to the alliance; what is named is displeasure and a state of remaining, with the causation running from what was sent. That framing recurs across the Quran and changes the register of judgement: less a courtroom than a delivery, and the shipment was made by the person receiving it.

crossReferences.why: Says every soul will know what it sent on ahead and what it held back.
Instructs a soul to look carefully at what it has sent forward for tomorrow.
Sets out the instruction about allegiance that this ayah describes being disregarded.

studies.applyIt: Ask what you sent ahead this week. Not what you meant, what actually left: the message you sent, the money you moved, the hour you gave someone. Make a short list on Friday. It is a strange and clarifying exercise, and it takes the question of character out of the realm of intention.

studies.title: Belief That Changes Nothing
studies.meaning: A test is proposed and it is behavioural. Had they believed in God, and the Prophet, and what was sent down to him, they would not have taken those others as protectors. The reasoning runs backward from conduct to conviction rather than forward, which is the reverse of how belief is usually assessed. The closing clause states the conclusion in the surah's characteristic register: not all of them, but many, have stepped outside the boundary.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the passage about alliances formed during a period of conflict. The commentators read this ayah as the summary of an argument begun several ayat earlier, and note that it supplies reasoning the earlier ayat had only implied. The setting throughout is a city in which whom a person stood with was public knowledge and could not be separated from what they claimed to hold.

keyTerms.note: A verb of adopting or acquiring, used across the Quran for taking something as a protector, a god or a friend. It describes a deliberate acquisition rather than a relationship a person drifted into over time.

The term used here rather than the word for messenger, and the commentators note that the surah alternates between the two. This one emphasises the office itself rather than the act of carrying a message.
From a root describing a date leaving its skin. Its repeated use across this section keeps naming one failure: not denial of a boundary but movement past one that is still acknowledged as real.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Nothing in that society was private. A visit, a gift, a marriage negotiation, a shared meal with a rival house: all of it was observed and discussed, and a man's alignment could be read from a season's ordinary movements. The idea that conviction could be inferred from conduct was not a theological claim to that audience; it was simply how everyone assessed everyone else.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah names God, the Prophet, and what was sent down as three objects of a single verb for believing. That triple construction occurs in a handful of places in the Quran and always joins the source, the carrier and the content together, which keeps any one of the three from being affirmed on its own.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage reasons from action back to belief and treats the inference as sound. That is a demanding standard, since it means a stated conviction can be checked against a record rather than only against a person's own sense of themselves. The surah applies the test to the community being addressed, and the commentaries read it as available to anyone examining their own alignments honestly.

crossReferences.why: Describes the conduct that this ayah then reasons backward from to its cause.
Sets a person's attachments against God and His Messenger and asks which is more beloved.
Says you will not find people who believe in God taking as friends those who oppose Him.

studies.applyIt: Take one belief you would say you hold firmly, and find the calendar entry from last month that reflects it. If there is not one, that is information rather than a verdict. Put one in this month. The ayah's method is to read conviction from conduct, and it works just as well turned inward.

studies.title: Because They Are Not Arrogant
studies.meaning: An observation is made about who stands closest and who stands furthest, and then the ayah does something unusual: it gives its reason. Those nearest in affection are described as saying we are Christians, and the explanation offered is that among them are priests and monks, and that they are not arrogant. The criterion named is a disposition rather than an identity, and the ayat that follow describe a specific encounter instead of a general rule.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical commentators connect this passage to particular Christian communities in the Prophet's lifetime, including those who received emigrants from Mecca and delegations that reached the city, and they read the ayat that follow as describing one such encounter; the reports differ in detail. The surah has qualified its descriptions of every community repeatedly, and does so again here by giving a reason.

keyTerms.note: A word for love carrying closeness and goodwill rather than passion. It is from the same root used for what God places between spouses, so what is described is a settled warmth rather than a political alliance.
From a root meaning to fear or to hold in awe. The word names people defined by a posture toward God rather than by an office, which is why it sits so naturally beside the clause about arrogance.
A form meaning to make oneself great, so what is denied is self-inflation rather than pride felt. The Quran uses this exact verb for refusing to accept truth from someone regarded as beneath one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Monastic cells dotted the trade roads through Syria and northern Arabia, and travellers relied on them. A monk gave water and shelter to a caravan and asked for nothing, which in that economy was remarkable enough to be remembered and retold. Traders returning to Mecca described these men, so the picture the ayah invokes was one its audience had heard about from people they knew.
studies.didYouKnow: The reason given in this ayah is stated grammatically as a cause, which is uncommon: the Quran usually describes conduct without explaining what produces it. Here the explanation is explicit and comes in two parts, the presence among them of people devoted to worship, and the absence of self-inflation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage grounds a difference in receptiveness rather than in identity, and it names the obstacle precisely: making oneself great. That is presented as what closes a person to what they hear, which matches the Quran's general account of why arguments fail to land. The reason is given openly, which makes the description portable, and any community can be measured by the same two markers.

crossReferences.why: Describes the encounter this ayah introduces, with eyes overflowing at what they heard.
Describes monasticism among the followers of Jesus and how it came about among them.
Describes those who make themselves great being turned away from the signs.

studies.applyIt: Notice whether you can accept a correction from someone you consider less qualified than you. That is the exact test this ayah names, and it is easier to fail than to detect. The next time it happens, take the correction on its merits and say thank you before you have finished deciding whether they were right.

studies.title: Eyes Overflowing With Tears
studies.meaning: A physical response is described before any decision is reported. When they hear what was sent down to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflow with tears, from what they have recognised of the truth. Recognition is the word used, not discovery: they are seeing again something they already held. Only then do they speak, and their request is not for entry or for reward but to be written down among those who bear witness.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The commentators connect this passage to a specific delegation that came to the city and heard the Quran recited, and reports name more than one such occasion without agreeing on which is meant. The surah has just explained why some listeners are open, and this ayah supplies the instance.
