Recitation was the ordinary way anyone encountered the text, so this scene describes the standard mode of first contact.

keyTerms.note: The verb of a vessel filling past its edge, used of a river in flood. It describes the tears as a consequence of something else being full, which locates the cause inside the person rather than in the eyes.

To know something again, distinct from the verb for coming to know a thing for the first time. The word implies prior acquaintance, which is why the commentators read the scene as recognition rather than discovery.
People who testify to what they have seen. The request is to be entered on a list of witnesses rather than of believers, which is a specific and notably modest thing to be asking for.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Poetry was recited aloud at fairs and gatherings, and audiences wept at it openly and without embarrassment. Arabia had a highly trained ear: people could tell within a few lines whether something was ordinary or extraordinary, and a strong recitation could silence a market. The reaction this ayah describes was culturally legible, which is part of why it is offered as evidence.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran describes weeping in response to hearing revelation in more than one place, and each time the physical response is given before any statement of belief is quoted. The order is consistent enough that the classical commentators remark on it, treating the tears as evidence rather than as a decoration of the scene.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats recognition as evidence and locates it in the body. Nothing is argued and nothing is conceded; something is heard and the eyes fill. That says something about how the Quran understands its own effect, and it sets a standard the surrounding argument cannot reach: a case can be resisted, but a recognition is hard to talk yourself out of once it has happened.

crossReferences.why: Gives the words they say next, arguing with themselves about why they should not believe.
Describes those given knowledge falling on their faces in tears at the recitation.
Describes those who fell down weeping when the signs of the Merciful were recited to them.

studies.applyIt: Listen to a recitation once this week without following a translation and without treating it as background. Five minutes is enough. You are not trying to feel anything in particular. This ayah describes a response that arrives before understanding, and most of us have arranged our listening so it never gets the chance.

studies.title: Why Should We Not Believe
studies.meaning: The speech continues, and it is framed as a question they put to themselves. What is it with us that we should not believe in God and in the truth that has come to us? The second half names what they want, and the verb is not certainty but longing: we hope that our Lord will admit us among the righteous. Nothing is claimed. A reason to believe is stated as the absence of a reason not to, and the outcome is left as a hope.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the account of a delegation's response. The commentators read this ayah as the reasoning behind the tears in the ayah before it, and note that the Quran quotes the speakers at length rather than summarising them. The surah does this repeatedly with both refusal and acceptance, giving each its own words and letting the two stand against one another.

keyTerms.note: An idiom asking what could possibly be the matter, used when a course of action needs no defence at all. The phrasing puts the burden of explanation on refusal rather than on assent.

A verb of eager desire that can also carry the sense of coveting. Used of God's mercy it names hope that reaches without presuming, which is why the classical commentaries treat it as the fitting posture.

keyTerms.gloss: the righteous, those who are sound
keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to be in good repair, the opposite of the word used elsewhere for corruption. The request is to be included among people who are whole rather than among those who are rewarded.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Admission to a group was a formal matter. A person joined a tribe by an act of alliance, was named in front of witnesses, and thereafter carried its protection and its obligations. Asking to be counted among a body of people, rather than asking for a benefit, was the natural way to phrase a request in that world, and this speech uses exactly that form twice over.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for hoping appears across the Quran for a longing that reaches upward without any assurance attached to it, and it is used of prophets and of ordinary people alike. It is one of the few words in the text that expresses desire toward God while explicitly not claiming a right to what is desired.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The speech models a posture the surah has been circling for many ayat: confidence about the truth and no confidence at all about one's own standing. Belief is stated as obvious and the outcome is stated as hoped for, and the two sit in a single sentence without tension. That combination is difficult to hold, and the passage presents it without comment.

crossReferences.why: Records Abraham hoping his faults will be forgiven on the day of judgement.
Gives the tears and the first request that this speech continues on from.
Records Joseph asking to be joined with the righteous, using the same phrase.

studies.applyIt: Try asking for something this week the way this speech does: state plainly what you believe, then name what you want as a hope rather than as an expectation. Most of our requests are either demands or apologies. This one is neither, and the difference is audible when you say it out loud.

studies.title: Rewarded For What They Said
studies.meaning: The response to the speech is a reward, and the ayah is precise about what is being rewarded: what they said. Not what they did, and not what they believed in the abstract, but the words just quoted. Gardens with rivers running beneath, and they remain there. Then the contrasting sentence arrives with no transition at all, naming those who rejected and denied. The two are set side by side and left without any comment joining them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the account of the delegation. The commentators note that the reward follows immediately on the quoted speech, which is unusual: elsewhere the Quran attaches outcomes to belief and to action, and here it attaches one directly to an utterance. The classical commentaries read the speech as evidence of what lay behind it rather than as sufficient by itself.

keyTerms.note: From the root meaning to return, so a reward is something coming back to its origin. The same root gives the word for a garment, which is put on and returns to its wearer, and the lexicographers note the connection.

The preposition marks cause. Attaching a reward to speech rather than to deeds is rare in the Quran, and the commentators are careful to read the words as evidence of a state rather than as a transaction.
From a root meaning good and beautiful at once. It names doing something well rather than merely correctly, which is a higher standard than the word usually rendered as righteous.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A spoken declaration carried legal weight in Arabia. A man became a member of a tribe, released a slave, divorced a wife or accepted a debt by saying so before witnesses, and there was no document behind any of it. Words were the instrument rather than the record of one. A reward attached to what someone said would have read as natural rather than as unusually generous.
studies.didYouKnow: The second of these two ayat is word for word identical with an ayah much earlier in the same surah, where it closes an entirely different passage. The Quran repeats fixed formulas this way at the ends of sections, and the classical commentaries treat such repetition as a structural marker rather than as emphasis.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing a reward on speech says something about how the Quran understands sincere utterance: it is not treated as separable from the person who produced it. The abruptness of the contrasting sentence matters too. Nothing softens the transition, and the effect is to keep the generous half of the passage from being read as a general amnesty while leaving the specific promise entirely intact.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same closing sentence word for word, ending a different passage in this surah.
Contains the speech that this reward is attached to as its stated cause.
Describes people of earlier scripture who believe, and names their reward with their Lord.

studies.applyIt: Say the thing you actually believe out loud to one person this week, in your own words rather than in borrowed ones. Not an argument, a statement. This passage attaches a great deal to an utterance, and most of us have never once put ours into a sentence we composed ourselves.

studies.title: Do Not Forbid The Good Things
studies.meaning: An instruction addressed to believers about their own strictness. Do not declare off limits the good things God has made lawful for you, and do not overstep. The commentators report that some in the community had begun renouncing food, rest and marriage as a form of devotion, and the passage stops it. What follows is positive: eat of what God has provided, lawful and wholesome, and be conscious of Him. Consciousness is placed alongside eating rather than against it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical commentators report that a group had resolved among themselves to give up meat, marriage and ordinary comfort in pursuit of devotion, and that these ayat came in response; the reports vary in their details and in who was involved. The general setting is a community in which enthusiasm was abundant and the shape it ought to take was still being worked out.

keyTerms.note: The verb of making something inviolable, in a form meaning to treat it as such. The instruction concerns the act of declaring rather than the act of abstaining, which is the distinction the commentators build on.

The verb of crossing a limit, used earlier in this surah of hostility toward others. Using it here for excess devotion places both under one description, as transgressions of a measure that was already set.
The same adjective this surah has used for permitted food and for clean earth. Its return here ties eating, purity and provision together through one word carrying pleasantness and cleanness at once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Renunciation was a recognised path in the region. Monks in the Syrian cells lived on very little, hermits were spoken of with awe, and the idea that closeness to God meant subtraction was in the air along every trade road. A community forming its own practice would naturally have reached for the model it could see, and this passage addresses that reach directly.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses this same verb for declaring something off limits when it criticises pre-Islamic practices of setting certain livestock aside. The instruction here therefore joins two apparently opposite errors, superstitious restriction and pious renunciation, under a single verb, on the ground that both take a decision that was never the person's to make.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage draws a line around a specific religious impulse. Enthusiasm that expresses itself by narrowing what is permitted is named as overstepping, and the word used is the one this surah applies to aggression. That places the two in one category: both take a measure belonging to God and adjust it. The positive instruction that follows keeps the correction from reading as permission to be careless.

crossReferences.why: Asks who has declared off limits the adornment and good provision God brought out for His servants.
Addresses declaring off limits something God had made lawful, in an entirely different setting.
Answers a question about what is permitted with a category rather than with a list.

studies.applyIt: Find one good thing you have quietly cut out of your life for reasons that sounded spiritual at the time: a food, a rest, a pleasure, a friendship. Take it back this week, deliberately and with thanks. This passage treats that reclaiming as obedience, which is not how most of us were taught to think about enjoyment.

studies.title: The Oaths You Did Not Mean
studies.meaning: A distinction is drawn between two kinds of oath. The idle ones, sworn without intent, carry nothing; the ones deliberately tied do. Then an atonement is set out, and it is given as a set of alternatives rather than as a single requirement: feeding ten needy people at the level you feed your own family, or clothing them, or freeing a person from bondage, and fasting three days for whoever can manage none of these. The closing instruction is to guard your oaths.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The commentators connect this passage to the ayat immediately before it, in which a group had bound themselves by oath to renounce ordinary comforts, and read it as providing the way out of an oath that should not be kept. Reports about the specific occasion vary. Oaths in Arabian life were sworn constantly and casually, which is the practice the first clause addresses.

keyTerms.note: Words carrying no weight, used elsewhere for chatter in a gathering. Naming a category of speech that does not bind is unusual, and it concedes that people talk without meaning what they say.
From the same root as the word for contracts in this surah's opening ayah. The image is a knot deliberately tied, so what makes an oath binding is an act rather than a particular form of words.

The middle of a range, and by extension the balanced or the best of it. Setting the standard at what you ordinarily feed your own household ties the atonement to the giver's actual life rather than to a fixed amount.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabs swore constantly. An oath punctuated ordinary speech the way emphasis does in English, and most of it meant nothing beyond insistence. But a formal oath, tied deliberately in front of witnesses, was among the strongest instruments in the society. Distinguishing the two was a practical necessity rather than a subtlety, because everyone produced both kinds within a single conversation.
studies.didYouKnow: The atonement is offered as three alternatives, with a fourth for anyone who can manage none of them, and the standard set for feeding is whatever the person ordinarily feeds their own household. That indexing of a requirement to the giver's own life rather than to a fixed quantity is a recurring feature of how the Quran handles atonement.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats speech as consequential and then immediately limits the consequence. Words that were not meant do not bind, which is a concession to how people actually talk; words that were tied do bind, and there is a way out of them that costs something. Both halves are needed. Without the first, ordinary conversation becomes a trap; without the second, a bad oath would have to be kept.

crossReferences.why: Draws the same distinction between idle oaths and what the hearts have deliberately earned.
Warns against making God a pretext in oaths against doing good and reconciling people.
Opens this surah with the instruction to fulfil what is tied, using the very same root.

studies.applyIt: Count how many times you say I swear or I promise in a day when you mean only that you are serious. Then, once this week, replace it with the plain sentence underneath. The passage takes both kinds of speech seriously enough to separate them, and separating them yourself takes about a day of noticing.

studies.title: Set It To One Side
studies.meaning: Four things are named together in one sentence: intoxicants, games of chance, the altars, and the divining arrows, and all four are described as defilement belonging to the adversary's work. The instruction given is to keep clear of them. Then the next ayah supplies the reasons, and they are social rather than abstract: the sowing of enmity and hatred among you, and being turned away from remembrance of God and from prayer. It closes as a question rather than as a command.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical commentators describe a sequence of passages on this subject revealed at intervals, of which this is the last, and note that the community's practice changed in stages. Reports about the immediate occasion vary. Wine and games of chance were woven into Arabian social life and into its poetry, which is why the passage argues from consequences rather than simply naming the thing.

keyTerms.note: A word for filth, used of what is physically and morally repellent at once. Applying it to all four items in the list places a drink, a game and a shrine practice under one single description.

From the word for a side, so literally to put something to one side of yourself. The verb asks for distance rather than for struggle, which is a different instruction from resisting something at close range.

A participle inside a question rather than an imperative, placed at the very end of the passage. The commentators note that the community treated the question itself as decisive, and the form leaves the answer to the hearer.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wine and the arrow game were social institutions. The game distributed shares of a slaughtered camel by lot and was regarded as generous, since winners fed the poor from their portions, and poets praised men for playing it. Drinking gatherings were where alliances were made and verse recited. Withdrawing from both meant withdrawing from the ordinary machinery of Arabian sociability.
studies.didYouKnow: The reason given in the second ayah is entirely social and devotional: enmity between people, and distraction from remembrance and from prayer. No physical harm is mentioned anywhere in it. The passage argues from what these practices do to a community and to attention, which is an unusual line of reasoning for its subject.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage names the harm rather than only the thing, and both harms it names are relational. Something that sets people against one another and something that pulls attention away from God are treated as two aspects of a single damage. Ending on a question rather than a command is also striking: the case is set out in full and the decision is then handed back to the listener.

crossReferences.why: Says there is benefit in them and greater harm, weighing the two against each other openly.
Addresses approaching prayer while not knowing what it is you are saying.
Names the divining arrows earlier in this surah, inside a quite different list.

studies.applyIt: Identify the thing that most reliably takes an evening from you and gives nothing back. You know which one. Put it physically to one side for a week, out of reach rather than resisted, and notice what fills the hours. This passage asks for distance rather than willpower, and distance is much easier to arrange.

studies.title: Only Clear Delivery
studies.meaning: A short instruction closes the passage. Obey God, obey the Messenger, and be on your guard. Then a conditional that lifts weight rather than adding it: if you turn away, know that all that rests on Our Messenger is clear delivery. The sentence is addressed to the community, and its effect is to separate two responsibilities. What is conveyed is one person's charge; what is done with it afterwards belongs to everybody else.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the passage on intoxicants and games of chance. The commentators read the placement as deliberate: a difficult instruction is followed by a reminder that the Messenger's part ends at delivery. The community was being asked to change a deeply embedded social practice, and the ayah addresses the pressure that puts on the one doing the asking as much as on those being asked.

keyTerms.note: The verb of wariness before a known danger, with no object supplied. Leaving it unstated makes the warning general, and the commentators read it as caution about one's own slipping rather than about anything external.
The noun from the verb used earlier in this surah for conveying the message. It names arrival rather than speech, and pairing it with the word for clarity sets the whole standard for the office.
An active participle, so not merely clear but clarifying. Attaching it to delivery means the message must be made plain rather than simply issued, which places a real demand on the one carrying it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The distinction between carrying a message and enforcing it was familiar. A herald sent between tribes announced terms and withdrew; whether the terms were accepted was not his affair, and holding him responsible for the answer would have been thought absurd. That convention protected messengers, and the ayah invokes it at a moment when a very unwelcome message had just been delivered.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about clear delivery being all that rests on the Messenger appears in several places across the Quran, and it recurs at the end of passages where a demand has just been made. Its function is consistent: it closes a section by defining what the one delivering the message is and is not answerable for.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah relieves the messenger without relieving the audience. Nothing is withdrawn from the instruction that precedes it; what is removed is any expectation that compliance was the messenger's to secure. That protects the office from being judged by results, and it also closes off a way of evading the instruction, since it makes clear that nobody else is going to carry it for you.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle a few ayat later in almost identical terms.
Says that if they turn away, only clear delivery rests upon you.
Divides the charge in two: his part is to deliver, and yours is to respond.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you have said clearly to someone once and are still repeating. Say it a final time, plainly, and then stop. The repetition is usually about your discomfort rather than their understanding, and this ayah draws exactly that line: delivery is your part, and the rest was never yours.
